2	## accessibility
3	accessibility-01 | Audit every screen with an accessibility inspection tool to find problems and see how the app presents itself to assistive technology.
4	accessibility-03 | Let people enlarge text and icons, ideally to at least twice the default size, and keep the interface working at that size.
5	accessibility-06 | Text and icons must reach WCAG AA contrast against their background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large (18 pt) or bold text.
6	accessibility-07 | When the desktop asks for higher contrast, switch to a scheme that meets the minimum contrast even if the default does not.
7	accessibility-08 | Check contrast minimums in every appearance the app offers, light and dark alike.
8	accessibility-10 | Pair colour with a shape, icon or text whenever it signals a difference in function or a change of state.
9	accessibility-11 | Consider letting people choose their own colours for things like chart series so they can pick ones they can tell apart.
10	accessibility-12 | Give every element and piece of content a description a screen reader can speak.
11	accessibility-13 | Never carry dialogue or vital information by sound alone: offer captions, subtitles, audio descriptions or transcripts as fits the media, and let people adjust how that text looks.
12	accessibility-20 | Name interface elements so voice-control software can address them by what people see and say.
13	accessibility-22 | Test the app with keyboard-only access, pointer and switch alternatives and screen readers, and label every element so they work.
14	accessibility-25 | Make every control reachable and operable by step-by-step element navigation so switch-access tools can drive the app.
15	accessibility-31 | Avoid fast or blinking motion, and when the desktop asks for reduced motion, cut automatic and repeating animation, zooming, scaling and peripheral movement.
16	charting-data-04 | Give every chart screen-reader names for its values and parts and accessible elements for its interactions.
17	charting-data-09 | A visible summary does not replace accessible names for the chart's elements; provide both.
18	charts-11 | Every chart must be usable with a screen reader, with names for its parts and values, not just a picture.
19	charts-19 | Distinguish chart series and essential values by shape, pattern or label as well as colour, e.g. two different point shapes for the two blood-pressure readings.
20	charts-20 | Put a separator between adjacent coloured segments, such as the parts of a stacked bar, so each segment can be told apart.
21	charts-22 | Give screen-reader users an overview of each chart: its kind (bar, line ...), what each axis measures and the axis bounds.
22	charts-23 | Decide per chart whether screen readers get one name per mark, per group of marks, or a single summary (fine for a small chart inside a button that opens a larger one), and give every interactive element its own name.
23	charts-24 | Shape screen-reader names to the chart's job: summarise stretches when the overall shape matters (a route's climbs), name each bar when exact per-period values matter (daily steps).
24	charts-25 | In a mark's accessible name, give the context first (the date or place the value belongs to) and then the value, without repeating what the chart overview already says, such as the axis name.
25	charts-28 | Name a series by what it stands for, not by its colour or shape, in accessible descriptions.
26	charts-30 | Leave visible axis and tick labels out of the screen-reader tree, since mark names and the overview already carry those values.
27	color-08 | Anything signalled by colour (state, object identity, interactivity) must also be signalled by text or a shape, so colour-blind people get the same information.
28	color-09 | Keep text and icons in enough contrast with their background, and avoid colour pairs that colour-blind people cannot tell apart.
29	dark-mode-03 | Every screen is checked for legibility in dark appearance with increased contrast and reduced transparency, separately and combined.
30	dark-mode-06 | Text and its background have at least 4.5:1 contrast in every appearance, with 7:1 the goal for small text in custom colours.
31	design-principles-13 | Treat accessibility as a requirement from the start, for the full range of people who may use the app.
32	feedback-02 | Deliver feedback through more than one channel (text, colour, sound) so people get it with sound off, eyes away or a screen reader.
33	gauges-01 | A gauge has short labels for its current value and its minimum and maximum, which screen readers announce.
34	icons-09 | Give every meaningful icon an accessible name that screen readers speak.
35	inclusion-17 | Support the platform's accessibility features such as the screen reader, display accommodations, captions and switch control.
36	inclusion-18 | Make every feature accessible rather than assuming some audience with a disability would not use it.
37	inclusion-21 | Keep interactions familiar and consistent, and make content perceivable by sight, hearing or touch alone.
38	motion-02 | No information is conveyed by animation alone, and the app works fully with reduced motion turned on.
39	notifications-14 | Anything important in a notification must also be shown as text; sound only adds to it.
40	text-views-03 | Check text views with the person's text-size and bold-text settings turned on.
41	toggles-04 | Make on and off clearly different by fill, shape or a mark such as a check or dot, never by colour alone.
42	typography-04 | Check that every piece of text stays readable in each place and platform it appears, and fix any that tests as hard to read.
43	typography-07 | When the person changes the text or interface size, headings must still read as more prominent than body text and secondary text as less.
44	typography-09 | A larger text setting should enlarge the content people read first (document text, messages) and may leave chrome such as tab titles at their size.
45	typography-16 | Text drawn in an app's own font must still respond to the person's text-size and bold-text settings, or the app offers its own text-size control.
46	
47	## commands
48	context-menus-01 | A context menu lists only the commands most likely wanted for the clicked item (e.g. Reply and Move for a message), not advanced or rarely used ones.
49	context-menus-02 | Keep context menus short enough to scan at a glance without scrolling.
50	context-menus-04 | Every context-menu command is also reachable from the main interface (menu bar, toolbar or buttons); on a Mac the menu bar lists all of them.
51	context-menus-05 | A context menu has at most one level of submenu, never a submenu inside a submenu.
52	context-menus-07 | Leave commands that do not apply out of a context menu entirely instead of showing them disabled; on a Mac, Cut, Copy and Paste may still appear disabled.
53	context-menus-08 | Put the most used commands nearest the point where the menu opened, reversing the order when the menu opens upward.
54	context-menus-09 | Context menu items do not display keyboard shortcuts; the shortcuts appear in the main menus.
55	context-menus-10 | Group context-menu items with separators, using no more than about three groups.
56	designing-for-macos-03*M | Every command of the app is reachable from the menu bar.

300	toggles-10*M | Use a switch for a setting with large scope, such as one that turns a whole group of settings on or off; use checkboxes for individual settings.
301	toggles-14*M | When a choice has more than two mutually exclusive options, use radio buttons, each with its own label, rather than a checkbox.
302	toggles-16*M | A checkbox that controls subordinate checkboxes shows a mixed state when they differ, and on/off when they all agree.
303	toggles-17*M | Don't use a radio button's mixed state; show mixed state with a checkbox, or express states as more radio buttons.
304	toggles-18*M | Use radio buttons for exactly-one-of choices and checkboxes when several may be chosen.
305	toggles-19*M | Keep a radio group to about five options; beyond that, use a pop-up button.
306	toggles-20*M | Use one checkbox for a single on/off setting; use a pair of labelled radio buttons only when a checkbox would not make the two states clear.
307	toolbars-13 | Use the standard Back and Close buttons, shown as their usual icons rather than the words 'Back' or 'Close', and implement any custom version identically everywhere.
308	writing-23 | Label every input field and use placeholder text with an example or description of the expected format (e.g. 'name@example.com').
309	
310	## feedback
311	accessibility-15 | Whenever a sound signals something (success, error, where to act), show a visible signal for it too.
312	alerts-06 | A problem found at start-up, such as no network, is shown as a quiet label next to cached or placeholder content rather than an alert.
313	buttons-03 | Every button, including custom-drawn ones, shows a distinct pressed state while the mouse button or key is held so the press visibly registers.
314	charts-16 | When marks or axes change, signal it by more than animation, including a screen-reader announcement, so people with reduced motion or no sight also notice.
315	collections-06 | Visibly mark items being inserted, removed or reordered, so the change can be followed.
316	design-principles-07 | Make actions reversible (undo, go back) so a mistake never costs people their work or much time.
317	design-principles-12 | Show whether controls are available, signal when content changes, and use the standard alert and choice patterns.
318	drag-and-drop-05 | Make every drop undoable with Undo, returning everything to the state before the drag.
319	drag-and-drop-07 | Where Undo is impossible, offer another way to reverse the drop's effect, such as cancelling the share it started.
320	drag-and-drop-10 | Start a drag, and show an image of what is being dragged, once the pointer has moved a few points with the button held, and keep it under the pointer until the drop.
321	drag-and-drop-12 | Let the drag image preview the result (for instance the size a photo will take in the document, or a grouped stack with a count for several items), without changing it constantly or radically.
322	drag-and-drop-13 | Show an insertion point or highlight only over destinations that accept the dragged content, and nothing or an explicit 'not allowed' sign over those that don't.
323	drag-and-drop-14 | Remove a destination's highlight as soon as the drag leaves it, and when several destinations are possible, highlight only the one under the pointer.
324	drag-and-drop-15 | When a drop is refused or fails, show it, for instance by sending the item back to where it came from.
325	drag-and-drop-20 | When dropped content takes time to arrive, show progress and a placeholder where it will appear.
326	drag-and-drop-21 | When a drop starts a task such as printing, show that it began and report its progress.
327	drag-and-drop-23 | After a drop, leave the dropped content selected at the destination and clear the selection in the source (copy within a container or any drop to another container).
328	drag-and-drop-28*M | Show a count of the dragged items during a multi-item drag, and lower it when a destination accepts only some of them.
329	entering-data-09 | Check each value as soon as it is entered and report a problem at once, not after the whole form is submitted.
330	feedback-01 | Match how intrusive feedback is to how much it matters: show status passively where people can look, and interrupt only for things like possible data loss.
331	feedback-03 | Show status (last update, unread count) next to the things it describes so people see it without acting or leaving their context.
332	feedback-07 | Confirm completion only for significant tasks (such as a payment); for ordinary actions report only failures.
333	file-management-04 | Work is saved automatically at intervals while editing and when a document is closed or the app loses focus, without needing an explicit save.
334	file-management-24*M | With autosave off, an unsaved document shows a dot in its window's close button and beside its name in the Window menu.
335	file-management-25*M | With autosave on, no unsaved-changes dot is shown, since nothing needs the person's action.
336	file-management-26*M | An 'Edited' suffix in the title bar is allowed but must vanish the moment the document is saved, automatically or by hand.
337	launching-01 | Show a usable first screen within a couple of seconds of starting.
338	lists-and-tables-03 | A row that navigates stays highlighted while its content is shown; a row that picks an option marks itself with a check rather than a lasting highlight.
339	loading-01 | Never show an empty window while loading; display placeholders at once and replace them as content arrives.
340	loading-02 | Load in the background so the rest of the app stays usable during loading.
341	loading-03 | During an unavoidably long load, show useful content such as tips, sized to a realistic estimate of the remaining time.
342	loading-05 | Whenever loading takes more than a moment or two, show a progress indicator.
343	loading-06 | Use a determinate progress indicator when the duration is known and an indeterminate one only when it is not.
344	motion-01 | Animate only where the movement tells the person something; no decorative or excessive animation.
345	motion-03 | Back up animated feedback with another channel, such as a sound or a text change, where it carries meaning.
346	motion-04 | Motion follows the person's action: something revealed by sliding down is dismissed by sliding back up, not sideways.
347	motion-05 | Feedback animations are short and tied exactly to the action they confirm.
348	motion-06 | Controls the person uses many times a session do not animate on each use.
349	motion-07 | Input is never blocked until an animation ends; the person can act or skip it at once.
350	notifications-13 | A notification may play a sound, either a system alert sound or a short, distinctive custom one.
351	notifications-20 | The app icon's badge (Dock or taskbar) only ever shows the count of unread items, never weather, dates, prices or scores.
352	notifications-21 | Essential news shown by a badge must also be easy to find inside the app as soon as it opens, since badges can be turned off.
353	notifications-22 | Lower or clear the badge count as soon as the user views the corresponding items.
354	onboarding-08 | A splash screen, if any, stays only long enough to be taken in at a glance.
355	popovers-11 | When a popover switches between condensed and expanded content, it resizes in place so it does not look like a new popover replaced it.
356	printing-10*M | Show a preview thumbnail that updates as print settings change.
357	progress-indicators-01 | Any task whose length can be estimated shows a determinate indicator rather than an indeterminate one.
358	progress-indicators-02 | A determinate indicator advances at a pace that matches the real remaining work, never racing to 90 percent and then stalling.
359	progress-indicators-03 | A progress indicator never sits still while work continues.
360	progress-indicators-05 | An indeterminate bar becomes determinate as soon as the remaining work becomes known.
361	progress-indicators-06 | An operation keeps the same indicator shape from start to finish; a spinner is never swapped for a bar.
362	progress-indicators-09 | A long operation offers Cancel when stopping is harmless, and Pause alongside Cancel when cancelling would discard work done so far.
363	progress-indicators-13 | Background tasks and progress in tight spots (inside a field, next to a button) use a small spinner.
364	progress-indicators-14 | A spinner carries no text label, since the person just started the operation.
365	scroll-views-02*M | On a Mac, custom-scrolled content rubber-bands at its ends like system scroll views.
366	scroll-views-06 | When an operation such as Find selects content or moves the insertion point out of sight, scroll so it becomes visible.
367	scroll-views-07 | If the user has scrolled away from the caret and starts typing, scroll back to the caret immediately.
368	scroll-views-09 | When a command acts on a selection the user has scrolled away from, scroll the selection back into view before applying it.
369	scroll-views-10 | Automatic scrolling moves the minimum distance needed; if part of the target is already visible, it may not need to move at all.
370	search-fields-02 | Update results with each keystroke rather than waiting for Enter, when the search is fast enough.
371	searching-03 | Always show what is being searched, through the placeholder, a scope control or a title (e.g. the mailbox name).
372	sliders-05*M | Apply a slider's effect continuously while it is dragged, not only on release.
373	split-views-01 | In every pane on the path to the detail view, the selected item stays highlighted.
374	text-fields-09 | A field that accepts only certain input (for example digits) tells the person when they enter something else.
375	text-fields-10 | Validate an email address when focus leaves the field; validate a new user name or password before focus is allowed to leave.
376	token-fields-03 | Token suggestions appear after a short pause in typing, not on every keystroke, so they do not distract.
377	undo-and-redo-02 | After undo or redo, bring the affected content into view and mark it (e.g. scroll to a restored paragraph).
378	windows-09*M | The key window, other main windows and inactive windows must look different, and update when their state changes, so people see which window takes input.
379	
380	## help
381	alerts-37 | An alert can include a Help button that opens the relevant help page.
382	buttons-09 | Buttons, especially icon-only ones, show a short tooltip describing their action after the pointer rests on them briefly.
383	buttons-24*M | Open help from the standard round question-mark help button rather than a custom-looking control.
384	buttons-25 | A help button opens the help topic about the dialog or pane it sits in, and falls back to the help's top page only when no specific topic exists.
385	buttons-26*M | A window contains at most one help button.
386	charting-data-06 | When a chart presents data in an unfamiliar form, show people how to read it, for example by introducing its parts one at a time.
387	entering-data-12*M | When a field's content is clipped, hovering over it shows the full text in a tooltip.
388	inclusion-09 | Offer a step-by-step introduction for newcomers that others can skip straight past to the content.
389	offering-help-01 | Match help to the task: a short inline note for a one- or two-step task, a guided walkthrough for a long multistep one.
390	offering-help-02 | Help shown in the interface concerns the action the person is doing at that moment.
391	offering-help-03 | Every piece of in-app help can be closed or skipped in one step.
392	offering-help-04 | Help text and pictures match the input device and context the person is actually using.
393	offering-help-06 | Help content follows inclusive-language guidance.
394	offering-help-07 | Help explains what a standard control does in this app, not how such controls work in general.
395	offering-help-08 | A control or input method unique to the app is introduced briefly with a picture or short demo rather than long text.
396	offering-help-09 | Use a popover tip to keep the content flow, an inline tip when nearby content must stay visible, pointing at a control when the tip is about it.
397	offering-help-10 | A tip covers only a feature done in three actions or fewer.
398	offering-help-13 | Show a tip only to people who have not used the feature yet and could benefit from it.
399	offering-help-14 | With several tips, show at most one per interval, such as one a day.
400	offering-help-17 | A tip can carry a button that opens the feature's settings or further reading.
401	offering-help-18 | A tooltip describes only the control under the pointer, not its neighbours or the wider task.
402	offering-help-23 | A control that needs a long tooltip is a sign the control should be redesigned.
403	offering-help-26 | A control's tooltip can change with its state, e.g. different text when on and off.
404	onboarding-01 | Onboarding lets people safely try the action being taught rather than only reading about it.
405	onboarding-02 | Features are taught by small tips shown when the related task comes up rather than one up-front walkthrough.
406	onboarding-03 | A tip about a part of the window is shown next to that part.
407	onboarding-04 | A required introduction is short and asks people to remember very little.
408	onboarding-05 | A tutorial can be skipped.
409	onboarding-06 | A skipped tutorial is not shown again at later launches but stays reachable from Help or Settings.
410	onboarding-07 | Onboarding explains the app, not how to use the operating system or device.
411	panels-10 | In help text, call a panel by its title, adding 'window' when the title alone is unclear ('Fonts window'), never introducing 'panel' as a kind of window.
412	segmented-controls-12*M | Every segment of a segmented control has its own tooltip naming what it does.
413	sliders-10*M | Hovering over a slider's thumb shows a tooltip with its current value.
414	the-menu-bar-54*M | The Help menu is the last menu in the bar and starts with an 'App Help' item that opens the app's documentation.
415	the-menu-bar-55 | Separate the main help item from secondary entries such as release notes or registration with a divider.
416	the-menu-bar-56 | Keep the Help menu short; link to further material from inside the help content instead of adding menu items.
417	writing-22 | When text refers people to a setting, give a button or link that opens it instead of describing the path.
418	
419	## keyboard
420	accessibility-23 | Every part of the app must be reachable and operable with the keyboard alone.
421	accessibility-24 | Don't take over shortcuts the operating system or its accessibility features already define.
422	alerts-29 | When the person should read the alert before answering, give it no default button so Return does nothing.
423	alerts-31 | Esc cancels an open alert, and on a Mac Command-Period does too, in addition to its Cancel button.
424	buttons-14 | In a dialog, sheet or alert, make the likeliest choice the default button so Return activates it and closes the dialog.
425	charts-14 | Give keyboard and switch users a logical, predictable route through a chart's values, for example moving along the X axis in order rather than jumping around.
426	charts-15 | For a large dataset, let keyboard focus step between groups of values first, instead of forcing people through every single point.
427	design-principles-15 | Make everything work with several inputs, including keyboard and pointer, not one alone.
428	designing-for-macos-05 | Provide keyboard shortcuts and make the whole app usable from the keyboard alone.
429	drag-and-drop-19*M | Read the modifier at the moment of the drop: Option held then turns a same-container move into a copy, and releasing it before the drop keeps it a move.
430	focus-and-selection-01 | Moving focus to an item may also select it, except where selecting would cause a context change such as opening a new view; then selection needs a separate action.
431	focus-and-selection-03 | Never move keyboard focus on the app's own initiative; focus changes only in response to the person.
432	focus-and-selection-04 | If the focused item disappears while the person is navigating by keyboard, move focus to a neighbouring item; otherwise hide the focus indicator.
433	focus-and-selection-05 | Follow the platform's rule for what takes focus: on a Mac, content elements (list items, text and search fields) take focus and buttons, sliders and toggles are reached via full keyboard access.
434	focus-and-selection-07 | Show focus on a text or search field with a ring, and in a list or collection by highlighting the whole row.
435	going-full-screen-14*M | Full screen starts only at the user's request, through the window's full-screen button, View > Enter Full Screen or Control-Command-F.
436	keyboards-01 | Every window, menu, control and feature must be reachable and operable with the keyboard alone, and this is checked by using the app with no pointing device.
437	keyboards-03 | A frequent app-specific action gets a newly chosen shortcut instead of borrowing one that already stands for a different action across the system.
438	keyboards-04 | A standard shortcut is reassigned only when its usual action cannot exist in the app, e.g. an app without text styling may use Command-I for Get Info instead of Italic.
439	keyboards-05*M | On a Mac the app honours Apple's standard map: Cmd-N new, O open, S save, Shift-Cmd-S save as/duplicate, W close window, Shift-Cmd-W close file, Opt-Cmd-W close all, P print, Shift-Cmd-P page setup, Q quit, H hide app, Opt-Cmd-H hide others, M minimize, Opt-Cmd-M minimize all, Z undo, Shift-Cmd-Z redo, X/C/V cut/copy/paste, Shift-Cmd-V paste as, A select all, Shift-Cmd-A deselect, F find, G and Shift-Cmd-G find next/previous, E use selection for find, Opt-Cmd-F go to search field, J scroll to selection, Cmd-comma settings, Cmd-? help, Cmd-` and Shift-Cmd-` next/previous window, B/I/U bold/italic/underline, T fonts, Shift-Cmd-C colours, Opt-Cmd-I inspector, Opt-Cmd-T toggle toolbar, Ctrl-Cmd-F full screen, Esc and Cmd-period cancel, Tab/Shift-Tab and Ctrl-Tab/Ctrl-Shift-Tab move focus between controls and control groups, Ctrl-arrows move between cells, Shift/Opt-Shift/Shift-Cmd-arrows extend the selection by character/word or paragraph/line or document; system-reserved keys (Cmd-Space, Cmd-Tab, Ctrl-F1 to F7, Shift-Cmd-3/4 screenshots, Opt-Cmd-Esc, Opt-Cmd-D) are never taken.
440	keyboards-06*M | On a Mac, Ctrl-Space, Ctrl-Opt-Space, any modifier plus Cmd-Space, and Cmd-Left/Right arrow stay free because the system uses them to switch input sources and keyboard layouts.
441	keyboards-07 | Only the few app-specific commands people use most get new shortcuts; rarer commands are reached through menus.
442	keyboards-08 | Modifiers keep their conventional effects during direct manipulation: the primary modifier while dragging moves items as a group, Shift while resizing keeps the aspect ratio, and a held arrow key nudges the selection by the smallest unit until released.
443	keyboards-09*M | Mac custom shortcuts are built on Command, add Shift for a related variant, use Option only for rare or expert commands, and avoid Control because the system claims it.
444	keyboards-10 | A shortcut that needs a modifier beyond the primary one pairs it only with letters A to Z, never with punctuation that some layouts type only with a modifier (French Option-5 gives '{').
445	keyboards-13 | Shortcuts are matched and displayed for the keyboard layout actually connected, and direction-bound shortcuts swap sides when the interface runs right to left.
446	keyboards-14 | Adding a modifier to an existing shortcut yields only a related command; e.g. Shift-Cmd-Z must stay tied to undo/redo, never an unrelated action.
447	scroll-views-01 | Every scrollable view responds to the mouse wheel, trackpad scrolling and the standard keys (arrows, Page Up/Down, Home/End, Space) exactly as system views do.
448	search-fields-20*M | Navigating to a dedicated search area puts keyboard focus in its search field.
449	settings-03 | Open settings by the platform's usual route, such as Command-Comma on a Mac (or Esc in a game).
450	text-fields-08 | Tab moves focus between fields in reading order.
451	the-menu-bar-05 | Every standard menu item the app includes (Cut, Copy, Paste, Save, Print and so on) answers to the platform's standard shortcut for it.
452	the-menu-bar-06 | Add a non-standard shortcut only when a command truly needs one, rather than giving every command a key combination.
453	the-menu-bar-59 | An alternate menu item appears with one modifier key held, never a combination.
454	token-fields-02 | Typed text becomes a token on a comma and also on other natural keys such as Return.
455	undo-and-redo-09*M | Undo and Redo are the first items of the Edit menu, on Command-Z and Shift-Command-Z.
456	
457	## layout
458	boxes-01 | Keep a grouping box clearly smaller than its window; a box that nearly fills it no longer reads as a group.
459	boxes-02 | Show sub-groups inside a box with spacing and alignment rather than nested boxes.
460	buttons-01 | Leave clear space between a button and neighbouring controls or content so it reads as a separate target and is easy to hit with any input.
461	buttons-06 | Buttons offered together as alternatives are the same size; the preferred one is set apart only by a more prominent style.
462	buttons-20*M | Buttons that act on one view, such as adding or removing table rows, sit directly inside or under that view so their target is unambiguous.
463	buttons-21*M | View-attached add/remove buttons never go in the toolbar or status bar; toolbar commands use toolbar items.
464	buttons-27*M | Place the help button in a dialog with OK/Cancel at the bottom corner opposite those buttons and aligned with them; in a dialog without dismiss buttons or in a settings window or pane, at the lower-left or lower-right corner.
465	buttons-28*M | The help button lives inside the content area, never in the toolbar or status bar.
466	buttons-30*M | Picture-only buttons belong in the content area; a toolbar uses toolbar items instead.
467	buttons-33*M | When an image button needs a caption, the caption goes underneath the image.
468	charting-data-01 | When people only need the data itself rather than insight into it, show it as a scrollable, searchable, sortable list or table instead of a chart.
469	charting-data-03 | Keep charts sparse and reveal more data or functions on request, e.g. by letting people pick a level of detail or a subset.
470	charting-data-10 | Size a chart to what it must show and support: large enough for its labels and interaction, small only for glanceable previews that open a fuller version.
471	charts-06 | Choose how many grid lines and axis labels to show from the chart's tasks: enough to estimate a value, few enough not to bury the data, and fewer still when people can inspect points directly.
472	charts-09 | Make the data the most prominent part of a chart, with axes and descriptions present as supporting context that does not compete with it.
473	charts-10 | When space is tight, give the plot as much width as possible: keep vertical-axis labels short, move units into the title, and place long category names inside the plot where they hide nothing.
474	charts-17 | Line a chart's leading edge up with the leading edge of the other content on the screen.
475	charts-18 | To keep that leading edge clean, put value-axis labels on the trailing side or on the trailing side of grid lines, and tie any floating label to its grid line with a tick.
476	collections-01 | Lay out collections as a plain row or grid, not a novel custom arrangement.
477	collections-02 | Present mainly textual items in a scrolling list or table, not a grid.
478	combo-boxes-05 | Size the combo box so no list item is truncated in its field.
479	design-principles-04 | Take people directly to their task or content and keep the interface unobtrusive.
480	design-principles-14 | Keep content and controls in the same predictable places across platforms and window sizes, easing transitions between states.
481	design-principles-17 | Keep the important things at hand and let the rest recede, without stripping useful function.
482	design-principles-19 | Use recognisable controls and a consistent structure that show where people are and what comes next.
483	designing-for-macos-01 | On large screens show more at once, with fewer nested levels and fewer modal steps, while keeping density comfortable.
484	disclosure-controls-01 | Show the most used options at all times and put advanced options behind a collapsed disclosure control.
485	disclosure-controls-03 | A disclosure button sits next to the control or area whose extra options it expands.
486	going-full-screen-02 | In full screen, use the extra room by adjusting proportions while keeping the same set of elements, with changes small enough that switching modes is not jarring.
487	going-full-screen-08 | When content is the focus in full screen (photos, reading), toolbars and navigation may hide temporarily.
488	going-full-screen-10 | Controls needed to navigate or complete the current task are never auto-hidden.
489	layout-01 | The most important items sit toward the top and the leading edge (left in left-to-right, right in right-to-left), since people scan in reading order.
490	layout-02 | Screens are built from library components that mirror themselves for right-to-left languages rather than from hand-placed parts that would need separate mirroring.
491	layout-03 | Related items share a common alignment edge, and only items that are subordinate to the one above them are indented.
492	layout-04 | Related controls and information are kept together and set apart from unrelated ones by space, a container or a separator.
493	layout-05 | Secondary content and choices start hidden behind disclosure triangles, menus, nested views or scrolling sections so the first view stays short.
494	layout-10 | Resizing a window or moving it to another display rearranges the layout within standard margins while keeping it recognisably the same.
495	layout-11 | At larger text or interface sizes the layout reflows: side-by-side parts stack, rows grow taller, single-line rows wrap, and no text is clipped or overlaps.
496	layout-13 | Every screen is checked for clipping at its smallest and largest window size, at the smallest and largest interface size, and in the longest localization.
497	layout-15 | Layout decisions are made from the space the window actually has, never from the operating system, device or screen it runs on.
498	layout-16 | Layouts are designed and tested for wide-and-short and narrow-and-tall windows, not only the default shape.
499	layout-17 | Narrowing a window may move commands into an overflow menu or collapse a sidebar, but every function stays reachable at every size.
500	layout-19 | Nothing essential, control or critical information, lives only along a window's bottom edge, because windows are often dragged partly below the screen.
501	layout-20*M | On a Mac with a notch, a full-screen window keeps content out of the camera housing area at the top.
502	lists-and-tables-01 | Use lists and tables for text-centred items; use a grid or collection for items of varying size or many images.
503	lists-and-tables-05 | When a column can get narrow, truncate in the middle where the start and end both identify the item, e.g. long file names.
504	lists-and-tables-09 | Lay out each row's parts to fit what it shows, e.g. a small leading image followed by a short label.
505	outline-views-02 | In a multi-column tree, only the first column indents and has disclosure triangles; other columns show attributes of each row.
506	outline-views-04 | A tree with more than one column always shows headings; a single-column tree without one gets a label or other context.
507	outline-views-12 | Cell text too long for its column is shortened with an ellipsis in the middle, keeping start and end, rather than cut off.
508	panels-14 | Keep floating overlay panels small, never covering the content they adjust or competing with it for attention.

## accessibility
accessibility-01 | Audit every screen with an accessibility inspection tool to find problems and see how the app presents itself to assistive technology.
accessibility-03 | Let people enlarge text and icons, ideally to at least twice the default size, and keep the interface working at that size.
accessibility-06 | Text and icons must reach WCAG AA contrast against their background: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large (18 pt) or bold text.
accessibility-07 | When the desktop asks for higher contrast, switch to a scheme that meets the minimum contrast even if the default does not.
accessibility-08 | Check contrast minimums in every appearance the app offers, light and dark alike.
accessibility-10 | Pair colour with a shape, icon or text whenever it signals a difference in function or a change of state.
accessibility-11 | Consider letting people choose their own colours for things like chart series so they can pick ones they can tell apart.
accessibility-12 | Give every element and piece of content a description a screen reader can speak.
accessibility-13 | Never carry dialogue or vital information by sound alone: offer captions, subtitles, audio descriptions or transcripts as fits the media, and let people adjust how that text looks.
accessibility-20 | Name interface elements so voice-control software can address them by what people see and say.
accessibility-22 | Test the app with keyboard-only access, pointer and switch alternatives and screen readers, and label every element so they work.
accessibility-25 | Make every control reachable and operable by step-by-step element navigation so switch-access tools can drive the app.
accessibility-31 | Avoid fast or blinking motion, and when the desktop asks for reduced motion, cut automatic and repeating animation, zooming, scaling and peripheral movement.
charting-data-04 | Give every chart screen-reader names for its values and parts and accessible elements for its interactions.
charting-data-09 | A visible summary does not replace accessible names for the chart's elements; provide both.
charts-11 | Every chart must be usable with a screen reader, with names for its parts and values, not just a picture.
charts-19 | Distinguish chart series and essential values by shape, pattern or label as well as colour, e.g. two different point shapes for the two blood-pressure readings.
charts-20 | Put a separator between adjacent coloured segments, such as the parts of a stacked bar, so each segment can be told apart.
charts-22 | Give screen-reader users an overview of each chart: its kind (bar, line ...), what each axis measures and the axis bounds.
charts-23 | Decide per chart whether screen readers get one name per mark, per group of marks, or a single summary (fine for a small chart inside a button that opens a larger one), and give every interactive element its own name.
charts-24 | Shape screen-reader names to the chart's job: summarise stretches when the overall shape matters (a route's climbs), name each bar when exact per-period values matter (daily steps).
charts-25 | In a mark's accessible name, give the context first (the date or place the value belongs to) and then the value, without repeating what the chart overview already says, such as the axis name.
charts-28 | Name a series by what it stands for, not by its colour or shape, in accessible descriptions.
charts-30 | Leave visible axis and tick labels out of the screen-reader tree, since mark names and the overview already carry those values.
color-08 | Anything signalled by colour (state, object identity, interactivity) must also be signalled by text or a shape, so colour-blind people get the same information.
color-09 | Keep text and icons in enough contrast with their background, and avoid colour pairs that colour-blind people cannot tell apart.
dark-mode-03 | Every screen is checked for legibility in dark appearance with increased contrast and reduced transparency, separately and combined.
dark-mode-06 | Text and its background have at least 4.5:1 contrast in every appearance, with 7:1 the goal for small text in custom colours.
design-principles-13 | Treat accessibility as a requirement from the start, for the full range of people who may use the app.
feedback-02 | Deliver feedback through more than one channel (text, colour, sound) so people get it with sound off, eyes away or a screen reader.
gauges-01 | A gauge has short labels for its current value and its minimum and maximum, which screen readers announce.
icons-09 | Give every meaningful icon an accessible name that screen readers speak.
inclusion-17 | Support the platform's accessibility features such as the screen reader, display accommodations, captions and switch control.
inclusion-18 | Make every feature accessible rather than assuming some audience with a disability would not use it.
inclusion-21 | Keep interactions familiar and consistent, and make content perceivable by sight, hearing or touch alone.
motion-02 | No information is conveyed by animation alone, and the app works fully with reduced motion turned on.
notifications-14 | Anything important in a notification must also be shown as text; sound only adds to it.
text-views-03 | Check text views with the person's text-size and bold-text settings turned on.
toggles-04 | Make on and off clearly different by fill, shape or a mark such as a check or dot, never by colour alone.
typography-04 | Check that every piece of text stays readable in each place and platform it appears, and fix any that tests as hard to read.
typography-07 | When the person changes the text or interface size, headings must still read as more prominent than body text and secondary text as less.
typography-09 | A larger text setting should enlarge the content people read first (document text, messages) and may leave chrome such as tab titles at their size.
typography-16 | Text drawn in an app's own font must still respond to the person's text-size and bold-text settings, or the app offers its own text-size control.

## commands
context-menus-01 | A context menu lists only the commands most likely wanted for the clicked item (e.g. Reply and Move for a message), not advanced or rarely used ones.
context-menus-02 | Keep context menus short enough to scan at a glance without scrolling.
context-menus-04 | Every context-menu command is also reachable from the main interface (menu bar, toolbar or buttons); on a Mac the menu bar lists all of them.
context-menus-05 | A context menu has at most one level of submenu, never a submenu inside a submenu.
context-menus-07 | Leave commands that do not apply out of a context menu entirely instead of showing them disabled; on a Mac, Cut, Copy and Paste may still appear disabled.
context-menus-08 | Put the most used commands nearest the point where the menu opened, reversing the order when the menu opens upward.
context-menus-09 | Context menu items do not display keyboard shortcuts; the shortcuts appear in the main menus.
context-menus-10 | Group context-menu items with separators, using no more than about three groups.
designing-for-macos-03*M | Every command of the app is reachable from the menu bar.
dock-menus-02*M | Every custom Dock menu command is also reachable from the menu bar or the window.
dock-menus-03*M | The Dock menu lists the app's open or recent windows so people can jump to one.
dock-menus-04*M | The Dock menu adds a few actions useful when the app is in the background or has no window, e.g. 'New Message'.
edit-menus-03 | Edit commands that cannot act are hidden or disabled: no Cut or Copy without a selection, no Paste with an empty clipboard.
edit-menus-04 | App-specific edit commands sit next to the standard commands they relate to, e.g. custom formatting after the standard formatting group.
edit-menus-05 | Keep the number of app-specific commands in the edit menu small.
edit-menus-08 | Edit menu actions run without confirmation and every one of them can be undone and redone.
edit-menus-09 | Do not add on-screen buttons for Cut, Copy, Paste and the like; the edit menu and standard shortcuts cover them.
edit-menus-10 | Keep Delete (removes, same as the Delete key) and Cut (copies to the clipboard, then removes) as distinct commands.
edit-menus-14*M | On a Mac, the menu-bar Edit menu lists its items in Apple's standard Edit menu order.
file-management-01 | A document app offers New and Open in its File menu with the standard New and Open shortcuts.
file-management-02 | Besides the menu command and shortcut, a visible add (+) button creates a new document.
going-full-screen-15*M | Do not add an app-specific menu for choosing window modes; rely on the standard full-screen commands.
image-wells-02 | An image well that supports copy and paste works through the Edit menu's Copy and Paste items and their standard shortcuts.
menus-05 | A command that cannot run now stays in its menu, drawn dimmed, and ignores activation instead of disappearing.
menus-06 | A menu whose items are all unavailable can still be opened so people can see what it holds.
menus-09 | Menu items get icons only for key actions, places, devices, visual operations or user content, and an item without a clearly fitting icon gets none.
menus-11 | The most used or most important items are placed at the top of a menu.
menus-12 | Related commands, e.g. Cut, Copy and Paste, form a group separated from other groups by a separator.
menus-13 | A rarely used command stays in the group of its related commands, e.g. Paste and Match Style next to Paste, rather than being moved elsewhere.
menus-14 | An overlong menu is split into several menus or shortened with a submenu.
menus-15 | A menu filled with user-made or generated entries, such as history or bookmarks, lists all of them and may scroll.
menus-16 | Submenus are used only where they clearly help, since each one hides its items.
menus-17 | When three or more items in a group share a leading term, they become one item named by that term with a submenu, e.g. 'Sort By' > Date, Score, Time.
menus-18 | Submenus go one level deep, and a submenu of more than about five items becomes its own menu.
menus-19 | A submenu item stays openable even when every command inside it is unavailable.
menus-20 | Subordinate menu items are put in a submenu, never indented under another item.
menus-21 | One menu item can switch its label with state, e.g. 'Show Map' becomes 'Hide Map' while the map is shown.
menus-23 | Where seeing both choices helps, both items are listed and the one that does not apply is unavailable.
menus-24 | Attributes that are on are marked with a checkmark beside their menu item.
menus-25 | Where several attributes can be combined, one item (such as Plain) clears them all at once.
notifications-15 | Notification buttons offer quick, common tasks that save opening the app, such as Snooze for a reminder.
notifications-17 | Do not add an 'Open' button to a notification; clicking the notification itself opens the related content.
notifications-18 | Notification buttons avoid destructive actions; if one is unavoidable, the notification gives enough context to know exactly what will be lost and the action is marked destructive.
panels-07*M | List panels in the Window menu only as show/hide commands, never among the document windows.
printing-01 | Put a Print… command in the File menu (in iOS, a toolbar button that opens the share sheet).
printing-02 | If the window has a toolbar, offer a Print button as an optional item people can add when customising the toolbar rather than a default one.
printing-03 | Disable the Print command (and any custom print button) when there is nothing to print or no printer is available.
pull-down-buttons-01 | A menu button lists only commands that refine its own action, e.g. Add listing what to add, Sort listing the sort keys.
pull-down-buttons-03 | A view's primary actions are visible buttons, not hidden inside one menu button.
pull-down-buttons-04 | A pull-down menu holds at least three items.
pull-down-buttons-05 | With only one or two items, use plain buttons for actions or toggles for settings instead of a menu button.
pull-down-buttons-06 | Keep a pull-down menu short enough to scan quickly.
pull-down-buttons-08 | A destructive item in a pull-down menu is marked as destructive and asks for confirmation in a separate prompt before running.
pull-down-buttons-10 | Give a menu item an icon, after its label, only when the icon clarifies the item.
searching-06 | Wherever search history is shown, offer a command to clear it.
settings-09*M | Put a Settings… item in the app menu that opens the settings window.
settings-10*M | Don't put a settings button in a window's toolbar; keep that space for frequent commands.
settings-11*M | Put a command for document-level options in the File menu.
sidebars-05 | Let people hide and show the sidebar with the platform's usual means, such as a toggle button or Show/Hide Sidebar commands in the View menu.
split-views-07*M | A hidden pane can be brought back by at least two routes, such as a toolbar button and a menu command with a keyboard shortcut.
the-menu-bar-01*M | Order the menu bar as: app-name menu, File, Edit, Format, View, any app-specific menus, Window, Help, leaving out only menus the app has no use for.
the-menu-bar-02*M | Include the standard menus in their standard order and make standard items such as Edit > Copy work on whatever text the user has selected in any text field.
the-menu-bar-03 | A menu's set of items never changes with context: an item that cannot act right now is shown disabled, not removed.
the-menu-bar-09*M | The app-name menu holds, in order: About App, Settings…, any app-level configuration items, Services, Hide App, Hide Others, Show All, Quit App.
the-menu-bar-12*M | Settings… opens only settings that apply to the whole app; settings that belong to one document are reached from the File menu instead.
the-menu-bar-13*M | Extra app-wide configuration commands sit directly after Settings…, inside the same separator group.
the-menu-bar-14*M | About App is the first item of the app menu and is followed by a separator so it forms a group of its own.
the-menu-bar-15 | An app that works with no files may drop the File menu or give it a name that fits what it does manage.
the-menu-bar-16*M | The File menu holds, in order and only where relevant: New Item, Open, Open Recent, Close, Close Tab, Close File, Save, Save All, Duplicate, Rename…, Move To…, Export As…, Revert To, Page Setup…, Print….
the-menu-bar-19 | Open Recent lists entries by recognisable document or file name only, never by full path.
the-menu-bar-20 | Open Recent is ordered by last opening time, newest at the top, and offers a Clear Menu item.
the-menu-bar-22 | When one file can be shown in several windows, offer Close File, which closes that file together with all its windows.
the-menu-bar-26*M | Offer Duplicate, which leaves both the original and the copy open, in preference to Save As, Copy To or Save To, whose effect on the original is unclear.
the-menu-bar-27 | Use Export As… only for writing a format the app does not normally open or save.
the-menu-bar-28 | After an export, the user stays in the original document and the exported file is not opened.
the-menu-bar-29 | Offer Page Setup… only when the app stores print settings such as paper size or orientation with each document.
the-menu-bar-31 | Put Find commands in the Edit menu when they search inside the current content; when they search for files or objects, the File menu may suit them better.
the-menu-bar-32*M | The Edit menu holds, in order: Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Paste and Match Style, Delete, Select All, Find, Spelling and Grammar, Substitutions, Transformations, Speech, then the system's Start Dictation and Emoji & Symbols.
the-menu-bar-35 | Delete removes the selection and leaves the clipboard as it was, unlike Cut.
the-menu-bar-36 | Paste inserts at the insertion point and leaves the clipboard intact so the same content can be pasted repeatedly.
the-menu-bar-37 | Leave out the Format menu when the app has no rich-text editing.
the-menu-bar-38*M | The Format menu holds Font (Show Fonts, Bold, Italic, Underline, Bigger, Smaller, Show Colors, Copy/Paste Style) and then Text (alignments, Writing Direction, Show/Copy/Paste Ruler).
the-menu-bar-39*M | Keep commands that switch between or manage windows out of the View menu; they go in the Window menu.
the-menu-bar-40*M | Have a View menu whenever any standard view command applies, even if it holds only Enter Full Screen.
the-menu-bar-42*M | The View menu holds, in order and as relevant: Show/Hide Tab Bar, Show All Tabs, Show/Hide Toolbar, Customize Toolbar, Show/Hide Sidebar, Enter/Exit Full Screen.
the-menu-bar-43*M | Place the app's own menus after View and before Window.
the-menu-bar-44 | Every custom command, including rarely used and advanced ones, appears in a menu-bar menu even when it is also reachable elsewhere in the app.
the-menu-bar-45 | Order custom menus to mirror how the app's objects contain one another, e.g. Mailbox, then Message, then Format.
the-menu-bar-46 | Arrange custom menus from the most general or most used to the least.
the-menu-bar-47*M | The Window menu holds no appearance or close commands: appearance goes in View and closing is File > Close.
the-menu-bar-48*M | Every app has a Window menu, even with a single window, including Minimize and Zoom so they can be reached from the keyboard.
the-menu-bar-49*M | Give each auxiliary panel a Window-menu item that shows or hides it, except panels the Format menu already opens.
the-menu-bar-50*M | The Window menu holds, in order: Minimize, Zoom, Show Previous Tab, Show Next Tab, Move Tab to New Window, Merge All Windows, Enter/Exit Full Screen (only without a View menu), Bring All to Front, then the open windows.
the-menu-bar-52*M | Enter/Exit Full Screen lives in the View menu; it moves to the Window menu only when there is no View menu, alongside separate Minimize and Zoom.
the-menu-bar-57 | Any command revealed only by holding a modifier while a menu is open must also be possible another way.
the-menu-bar-58 | Do not put modifier-revealed alternate items in context menus or dock/taskbar menus.
the-menu-bar-66*M | Clicking the menu bar extra opens a menu, not a popover, unless the function is too complex for a menu.
the-menu-bar-69*M | Anything the menu bar extra offers is also reachable elsewhere, for example from the Dock menu.
token-fields-01 | Each token offers a context menu with details or editing commands for it.
toolbars-04 | Put lower-priority actions in a More menu only when they cannot all fit in the toolbar itself.
toolbars-05 | In apps with many toolbar actions or long working sessions, let users choose which items the toolbar shows.
toolbars-14 | Fill the toolbar with the commands for the main tasks, usually the most frequent ones or those acting on the most important objects.
toolbars-15 | Every toolbar item's purpose is obvious without trying it.
toolbars-16 | Label toolbar items with recognisable icons, falling back to text for actions such as Edit that have no clear icon.
toolbars-31*M | Every toolbar command also exists as a menu-bar command, since the toolbar can be hidden or customised; the reverse is not required.
undo-and-redo-01 | Name the action in the Undo and Redo command labels (e.g. 'Undo Typing', 'Redo Bold').
undo-and-redo-03 | Keep an unlimited undo history at least back to the last open or save.
undo-and-redo-04 | Let a run of related small edits undo as one step, and offer a way to revert all changes since opening or saving.
undo-and-redo-05 | Rely on the Edit menu and the standard shortcuts for undo; add on-screen undo/redo buttons only when really needed.
undo-and-redo-06 | Dedicated undo and redo buttons go in the toolbar with the conventional undo/redo icons.
windows-03 | Offer an 'open in new window' command for content, in its context menu or the File menu.

## consistency
accessibility-26 | Use the platform's familiar, consistent interactions rather than custom ones people must learn and remember.
buttons-10 | Common actions such as share, delete or add use the icon people already associate with them, the same one everywhere in the app.
charting-data-05 | Prefer familiar chart types such as bar and line charts that people already know how to read.
charting-data-11 | Give charts with similar purposes the same type and style across the app, changing them only to signal a real difference.
charting-data-12 | Charts of the same dataset (a summary and its expanded view) keep the same chart type, colours, annotations, layout and wording.
charts-29 | Mention axes in the same order in every description across the app, e.g. always X before Y.
color-01 | Give each colour a single meaning across the app; a colour that marks interactive elements must never also style plain, non-interactive text.
color-12 | Use each semantic colour only for the role its name states, e.g. never draw text in the separator colour or fill a background with the secondary-label colour.
color-wells-01 | Every colour choice in the app opens the same colour picker so it behaves identically everywhere.
context-menus-03 | If one kind of object has a context menu, every comparable object in the app has one too.
context-menus-13 | When menu items carry icons, common actions such as Copy, Share and Delete use the same icon in every menu and toolbar of the app.
dark-mode-01 | The app follows the system's light or dark choice by default so people need not set appearance twice.
dark-mode-02 | The app is complete in both light and dark and switches between them live when the system changes appearance while it runs.
design-principles-10 | Base interactions on concepts people already know from the world and other software.
design-principles-11 | Once an element has a behaviour or look, give it the same one everywhere.
design-principles-16 | Give each supported platform equal care so the app feels native on each.
design-principles-22 | Keep updating the interface to current platform capabilities and patterns after release.
designing-for-macos-06 | Let users customise toolbars, choose which views a window shows, and pick the appearance they prefer.
edit-menus-01 | Editing commands appear in the standard edit menu with its usual contents, never in a separate custom menu repeating them.
file-management-05 | File names are shown without extensions unless the person opts to see them, and every open and save view follows that choice.
icons-11 | Use the conventional picture for each editing action wherever it appears: scissors for Cut, stacked pages for Copy, a page on a clipboard for Paste, a check for Done, an x for Cancel, a bin for Delete, back/forward U-turn arrows for Undo/Redo, square with pencil for Compose, two overlapping squares with plus for Duplicate, pencil for Rename, folder for Move to, paperclip for Attach, plus for Add, ellipsis for More.
icons-12 | Use a check in a circle for Select, an x for Deselect and a bin for Delete in selection modes.
icons-13 | Use the standard formatting pictures: raised/lowered small letters for Superscript/Subscript, B, I and U letterforms for Bold, Italic, Underline, and line-alignment pictures for Align Left, Center, Justified, Align Right.
icons-14 | Use a magnifying glass for Search, a page with a magnifier for Find, and a funnel of shortening lines for Filter.
icons-15 | Use a box with an upward arrow for Share/Export and a printer for Print.
icons-16 | Use a person in a circle for Account, User and Profile.
icons-17 | Use thumbs up for Like and thumbs down for Dislike.
icons-18 | Use stacked layers with the top or bottom layer filled for Bring to Front/Send to Back (three layers) and Bring Forward/Send Backward (two layers).
icons-19 | Use an alarm clock for Alarm, an archive box for Archive and a calendar page for Calendar.
inclusion-08 | The app must be usable without prior special knowledge, with an interface that matches each platform's conventions.
menus-08 | A common action such as Share, Print or Search uses the same icon wherever it appears in the app.
menus-26 | A custom-drawn menu responds to the same pointer and keyboard interactions as the platform's own menus.
notifications-23 | Do not draw your own badge-like counter on the icon or elsewhere to imitate the system badge.
pointing-devices-03 | Every task can be done with the mouse or with the keyboard alone, reaching the same result, so users can switch input mid-task without learning a second interaction model.
progress-indicators-08 | Progress for a given kind of operation always appears in the same place.
rating-indicators-02 | Use stars for ratings; use another symbol only if it clearly reads as a rating scale.
search-fields-16*M | Search is placed and behaves the same way on every desktop platform the app supports.
settings-05 | Follow system-wide preferences (accessibility, scrolling, authentication) and don't duplicate them as app settings.
toggles-12*M | Where the interface already uses a checkbox for a setting, keep the checkbox rather than swapping in a switch.
toolbars-25 | Toolbar groups and their positions are the same on every platform the app runs on.
writing-02 | Keep a glossary of the app's terms and use the same word for the same thing everywhere.
writing-10 | Reuse the same phrasing patterns for recurring kinds of text.

## controls
accessibility-29 | Never autoplay audio or video without visible start and stop controls, and consider a setting that turns autoplay off everywhere.
buttons-04 | Mark the action users are most likely to take in a view with the prominent button style and leave the others in the plain style.
buttons-05 | A view never shows more than two prominent-style buttons at once.
buttons-08 | Each button's icon, text or both must tell the user what it will do before they press it.
buttons-22*M | View-attached add/remove buttons carry an icon (plus, minus, etc.) rather than a text title.
color-07 | When people pick a colour, offer the platform's standard colour chooser rather than a home-made one, so saved colours are shared with other apps.
color-wells-02 | A colour swatch control shows it is active while its picker is open, updates to the chosen colour, and accepts colours dragged from other swatches or the picker.
column-views-01 | A column browser suits a deep hierarchy that people move up and down often and that needs no sorting; sortable data goes in a list or table.
column-views-02 | The first column always shows the top level of the hierarchy.
column-views-03 | Selecting a leaf item fills the next column with its details or preview, e.g. dates, type and size.
column-views-04 | Browser columns can be resized by the person so long names fit.
combo-boxes-01 | Start a combo box with a sensible value from its list (not necessarily the first) rather than empty.
combo-boxes-02 | Put a label before every combo box describing what it holds.
combo-boxes-04 | Fill the list with the most likely values while still accepting typed custom values.
disclosure-controls-04 | A view contains at most one disclosure button.
edit-menus-06 | Read-only content text, such as captions and statuses, can be selected and copied.
edit-menus-07 | Labels on controls are not selectable; content text is.
entering-data-01 | Accept every input method the platform offers for a field (typing, picking, pasting, dropping) so the user can use whichever suits them.
entering-data-04 | Prefill fields with sensible defaults wherever one exists.
entering-data-05 | Fields for passwords and other sensitive data mask each typed character.
entering-data-06 | A password field always opens empty; the user types it or uses the system's credential store.
entering-data-07 | When the valid answers are known, let users pick from a list, menu or picker instead of typing.
entering-data-10 | Numeric fields accept only numbers and display them in the intended format (decimals, percent, currency).
entering-data-11 | Keep Next or Continue disabled until every required field has a value.
gauges-03*M | A level indicator over a large range uses a continuous fill rather than discrete segments.
image-wells-01 | An image well that needs an image shows its default image again after being cleared.
inclusion-13 | Ask for gender only when required, and then offer choices beyond two plus a way to decline, optionally with pronouns.
labels-01 | Short read-only text is a label, short editable text a text field, and long text a text view.
labels-04 | Read-only text people may want to reuse, such as an error message, address or IP address, can be selected and copied.
layout-06 | Controls must be recognisable as controls and never be mistaken for the content they act on.
lists-and-tables-02 | Let users reorder list items where order matters, even when they cannot add or remove them.
lists-and-tables-15*M | Show nested data, such as folders and their contents, in an outline with expandable rows rather than a flat table.
outline-views-01 | Flat data goes in a plain table; an expandable tree is only for data with real parent-child structure.
outline-views-05 | Clicking a column heading sorts by it, clicking again reverses the order, and sorting by the first column sorts each level of the hierarchy separately.
outline-views-06 | Tree and table columns can be resized by dragging their heading dividers.
outline-views-08 | Remember which nodes are expanded and restore that state the next time the view is shown.
outline-views-11 | Where useful, rows can be reordered by dragging, added and removed.
outline-views-13 | A window built around a long tree offers a search field, usually in its toolbar.
panels-04 | Fill panels with direct adjustment controls such as sliders and steppers, avoiding text entry and select-then-act controls.
pickers-01 | Use a scrolling picker for medium-to-long lists of values.
pickers-02 | Offer a short list of choices in a menu button, and a very large set in a list or table, which can have an index.
pickers-03 | Order picker values so hidden ones are predictable (e.g. countries alphabetically).
pickers-04 | Show a picker in context, beside or below the field it edits or in a popover, never by moving to another view.
pickers-05 | Where exact minutes are not needed, step the minute list by a divisor of 60 (e.g. 0, 15, 30, 45).
pickers-07*M | Use a typed (textual) date field for precise entry in little space, and a calendar (graphical) picker for browsing days or choosing a range.
pop-up-buttons-01 | Use a pop-up (select) button for choosing one of several exclusive options, and show the chosen one on the button.
pop-up-buttons-02 | Use a pull-down menu button, not a pop-up button, for a list of actions, multiple selection or submenus.
pop-up-buttons-03 | Preselect the option most people will want.
pop-up-buttons-05 | Prefer a pop-up button over radio buttons when space is short and options need not all be visible.
pop-up-buttons-06 | Put rarely used extra choices behind a 'Custom' item instead of adding controls, optionally with explanatory text.
printing-08*M | Show when one print option rules out another, e.g. disable 'transparencies' when two-sided is chosen.
pull-down-buttons-02 | Picking one value from a set of options is a pop-up (select) button, not a pull-down command menu.
rating-indicators-01 | Let people change an item's rating directly in the list, without opening a separate edit screen.
right-to-left-07 | Sliders and progress indicators run from right to left in right-to-left layouts, with their start and end icons swapped too.
right-to-left-08 | Back, next and previous controls point the other way in right-to-left layouts, e.g. Back points right.
right-to-left-09 | A control meaning a physical direction, such as 'to the right', keeps pointing that way in every layout direction.
scroll-views-05 | Offer scrolling by one view-height page at a time where it suits the content, keeping a small overlap (e.g. one line of text) so the reader keeps their place.
scroll-views-11 | Zoomable views clamp zoom to sensible limits, e.g. text cannot be zoomed until one character fills the view.
search-fields-03 | Offer recent searches before typing starts and predicted terms while typing.
search-fields-05 | Provide a way, such as a scope bar above the results, to narrow search results quickly.
search-fields-06 | Use a scope bar only for distinct, well-defined categories that move the search from broad to narrow.
search-fields-07 | A search starts with the widest scope selected; the user narrows it.
search-fields-08 | Represent common filters (a person, a content type) as tokens in the field that can be selected and edited as a single unit.
search-fields-09 | Surface available tokens through search suggestions so users discover them.
searching-04 | Show recent searches before typing starts and suggestions while typing.
segmented-controls-01 | Use a segmented control only for a small set of closely related choices or actions on one object, state or view.
segmented-controls-02 | Choose a segmented control when the options must stay visibly grouped at any size or their selected state must be seen at a glance.
segmented-controls-03 | A segmented control either holds a selection or performs actions; never mix action segments with selectable ones.
segmented-controls-04 | Keep a segmented control to about five to seven segments at most on a wide window.
segmented-controls-06 | All segments of one control are labelled the same way: all text or all icons.
segmented-controls-13*M | Switch views in the main window area with tabs; reserve segmented view-switchers for toolbars and inspector panes.
sidebars-03 | With many sidebar entries, group them under collapsible disclosure headings.
sliders-02 | A horizontal slider has its minimum at the leading end and maximum at the trailing end; a vertical one has its minimum at the bottom.
sliders-03 | For wide ranges, pair a slider with a numeric field showing the exact value and a stepper for whole-number steps.
sliders-06*M | Use a linear slider between fixed end points (e.g. opacity 0–100%) and a circular one for values that wrap or continue (e.g. rotation).
sliders-08*M | Add tick marks to a slider when users need to judge the scale or hit specific values.
steppers-01 | Place a stepper directly beside the field showing the value it changes, so which value it affects is unmistakable.
steppers-02 | When values can vary widely, pair the stepper with an editable field, e.g. number of copies when printing.
tab-views-01 | Tabs hold panes whose content is related; unrelated content does not share a tab view.
tab-views-02 | A control inside a tab pane changes only that pane's content.
tab-views-05 | Pane switching uses a visible tab control, not a pop-up button, unless there are too many panes for tabs.
tab-views-06 | A tab view has at most six tabs; more panes call for another design, such as a pop-up menu of views.
tab-views-07 | The tab control is hidden only when the app itself, not the person, switches panes.
text-fields-01 | Use a single-line field for short entries like a name or address; longer text goes in a multi-line text view.
text-fields-02 | An empty field may show placeholder text naming what to enter, e.g. 'Email'.
text-fields-03 | Because placeholder text vanishes on typing, give the field a separate visible label too.
text-fields-04 | Passwords and other secrets are entered in a field that masks the characters.
text-fields-11 | Numeric fields accept only numbers and show them formatted (decimals, percent, currency).
text-fields-13 | Choose per field whether overflowing text clips, wraps, or is truncated with an ellipsis at start, middle or end.
text-fields-19 | When typed input should also offer a list of choices, use a combo box rather than a plain field.
text-views-01 | Use a multi-line text view for long, editable or formatted text; short text uses a label or, if editable, a text field.
text-views-04 | Text people may want to reuse, such as error messages, serial numbers and IP addresses, can be selected and copied.
toggles-01 | Use a toggle only to switch something between two opposite states; for picking from a list or other actions use another control, such as a pop-up button.
toggles-02 | Make it clear what each toggle turns on or off, from its context or from a label stating the setting.
toggles-03 | A button that acts as a toggle shows an icon for what it does and changes its appearance, such as its background, to show whether it is on.
toggles-10*M | Use a switch for a setting with large scope, such as one that turns a whole group of settings on or off; use checkboxes for individual settings.
toggles-14*M | When a choice has more than two mutually exclusive options, use radio buttons, each with its own label, rather than a checkbox.

toggles-19*M | Keep a radio group to about five options; beyond that, use a pop-up button.
toggles-20*M | Use one checkbox for a single on/off setting; use a pair of labelled radio buttons only when a checkbox would not make the two states clear.

## feedback
accessibility-15 | Whenever a sound signals something (success, error, where to act), show a visible signal for it too.

launching-01 | Show a usable first screen within a couple of seconds of starting.
lists-and-tables-03 | A row that navigates stays highlighted while its content is shown; a row that picks an option marks itself with a check rather than a lasting highlight.
loading-01 | Never show an empty window while loading; display placeholders at once and replace them as content arrives.

motion-01 | Animate only where the movement tells the person something; no decorative or excessive animation.
motion-03 | Back up animated feedback with another channel, such as a sound or a text change, where it carries meaning.
motion-04 | Motion follows the person's action: something revealed by sliding down is dismissed by sliding back up, not sideways.

search-fields-02 | Update results with each keystroke rather than waiting for Enter, when the search is fast enough.
searching-03 | Always show what is being searched, through the placeholder, a scope control or a title (e.g. the mailbox name).

text-fields-09 | A field that accepts only certain input (for example digits) tells the person when they enter something else.

buttons-24*M | Open help from the standard round question-mark help button rather than a custom-looking control.
buttons-25 | A help button opens the help topic about the dialog or pane it sits in, and falls back to the help's top page only when no specific topic exists.

panels-10 | In help text, call a panel by its title, adding 'window' when the title alone is unclear ('Fonts window'), never introducing 'panel' as a kind of window.
segmented-controls-12*M | Every segment of a segmented control has its own tooltip naming what it does.
sliders-10*M | Hovering over a slider's thumb shows a tooltip with its current value.

focus-and-selection-01 | Moving focus to an item may also select it, except where selecting would cause a context change such as opening a new view; then selection needs a separate action.

keyboards-05*M | On a Mac the app honours Apple's standard map: Cmd-N new, O open, S save, Shift-Cmd-S save as/duplicate, W close window, Shift-Cmd-W close file, Opt-Cmd-W close all, P print, Shift-Cmd-P page setup, Q quit, H hide app, Opt-Cmd-H hide others, M minimize, Opt-Cmd-M minimize all, Z undo, Shift-Cmd-Z redo, X/C/V cut/copy/paste, Shift-Cmd-V paste as, A select all, Shift-Cmd-A deselect, F find, G and Shift-Cmd-G find next/previous, E use selection for find, Opt-Cmd-F go to search field, J scroll to selection, Cmd-comma settings, Cmd-? help, Cmd-` and Shift-Cmd-` next/previous window, B/I/U bold/italic/underline, T fonts, Shift-Cmd-C colours, Opt-Cmd-I inspector, Opt-Cmd-T toggle toolbar, Ctrl-Cmd-F full screen, Esc and Cmd-period cancel, Tab/Shift-Tab and Ctrl-Tab/Ctrl-Shift-Tab move focus between controls and control groups, Ctrl-arrows move between cells, Shift/Opt-Shift/Shift-Cmd-arrows extend the selection by character/word or paragraph/line or document; system-reserved keys (Cmd-Space, Cmd-Tab, Ctrl-F1 to F7, Shift-Cmd-3/4 screenshots, Opt-Cmd-Esc, Opt-Cmd-D) are never taken.

combo-boxes-05 | Size the combo box so no list item is truncated in its field.
design-principles-04 | Take people directly to their task or content and keep the interface unobtrusive.
design-principles-14 | Keep content and controls in the same predictable places across platforms and window sizes, easing transitions between states.
design-principles-17 | Keep the important things at hand and let the rest recede, without stripping useful function.
design-principles-19 | Use recognisable controls and a consistent structure that show where people are and what comes next.

layout-01 | The most important items sit toward the top and the leading edge (left in left-to-right, right in right-to-left), since people scan in reading order.
layout-02 | Screens are built from library components that mirror themselves for right-to-left languages rather than from hand-placed parts that would need separate mirroring.

layout-15 | Layout decisions are made from the space the window actually has, never from the operating system, device or screen it runs on.
layout-16 | Layouts are designed and tested for wide-and-short and narrow-and-tall windows, not only the default shape.
layout-17 | Narrowing a window may move commands into an overflow menu or collapse a sidebar, but every function stays reachable at every size.
layout-19 | Nothing essential, control or critical information, lives only along a window's bottom edge, because windows are often dragged partly below the screen.
layout-20*M | On a Mac with a notch, a full-screen window keeps content out of the camera housing area at the top.
lists-and-tables-01 | Use lists and tables for text-centred items; use a grid or collection for items of varying size or many images.
lists-and-tables-05 | When a column can get narrow, truncate in the middle where the start and end both identify the item, e.g. long file names.
lists-and-tables-09 | Lay out each row's parts to fit what it shows, e.g. a small leading image followed by a short label.
outline-views-02 | In a multi-column tree, only the first column indents and has disclosure triangles; other columns show attributes of each row.
outline-views-04 | A tree with more than one column always shows headings; a single-column tree without one gets a label or other context.

panels-14 | Keep floating overlay panels small, never covering the content they adjust or competing with it for attention.
