509	path-controls-01 | Place a file-path bar inside the window's content area, never in the toolbar or status bar.
510	popovers-02 | Content needed only now and then goes in a popover rather than a permanent sidebar or panel.
511	popovers-03 | A popover points at the control that opened it and does not cover that control or content needed while using it.
512	popovers-10 | Size a popover to its contents and no larger.
513	printing-09*M | Hide rarely used print options behind a disclosure control labelled 'Advanced Options'.
514	right-to-left-01 | Text left-aligned in a left-to-right layout is right-aligned when the layout is mirrored.
515	right-to-left-02 | Text of three or more lines is aligned by its own script's direction, while one- and two-line text follows the interface direction.
516	right-to-left-03 | All items of a list share one alignment, following the interface direction even for items in another script.
517	right-to-left-05 | The digits of a single number, phone number or card number keep their order in right-to-left layouts.
518	right-to-left-06 | Scale numbers on mirrored sliders, progress bars and ratings, and ordered number sequences, run in reversed order, while each numeral's glyph stays unmirrored.
519	right-to-left-11 | Photos and illustrations are never mirrored for right-to-left; a direction-bound image gets a separate version instead.
520	right-to-left-12 | Images arranged in a meaningful order (by date, alphabet, rank) are laid out in reverse order in right-to-left layouts.
521	right-to-left-13 | Icons that depict text lines or reading direction are mirrored in right-to-left layouts.
522	right-to-left-16 | Icons that show something moving forward or backward are mirrored in right-to-left layouts so the motion keeps its meaning.
523	right-to-left-17 | Logos and universal marks such as the checkmark are never mirrored.
524	right-to-left-18 | Icons of real objects (clocks, right-handed tools) stay unmirrored unless they show a direction.
525	scroll-views-03 | When content continues past the view's edge, signal it, e.g. by letting a partly visible row or item show at the edge.
526	scroll-views-04 | Never nest a vertically scrolling region inside another vertical one (or horizontal in horizontal); crossing orientations is fine.
527	search-fields-04 | Rank results so the most relevant come first, and group them by category where that helps.
528	search-fields-17*M | A search that spans the window's content, especially in split views, sits at the trailing end of the toolbar.

780	sheets-14*M | A sheet blocks only its parent window: the app's other windows stay usable and can be brought forward while it is open.
781	sheets-15*M | Tasks that repeat input and check results, such as find and replace, use a non-modal panel rather than a sheet.
782	the-menu-bar-21 | In a window with tabs, where Close becomes Close Tab, also offer Close Window to shut every tab at once.
783	the-menu-bar-24 | The first save of a never-saved document asks for its name and folder.
784	the-menu-bar-25 | When a document can be saved in several formats, the format is picked from a drop-down inside the save dialog rather than through separate commands.
785	the-menu-bar-30 | Printer choice, copy count and other per-print or global options are set in the Print dialog, not in Page Setup.
786	the-menu-bar-51*M | Zoom toggles between a content-fitted size and the user's size; it never enters or leaves full screen.

789	windows-01 | Every window's layout must keep working as the window is resized, so it can share the screen with other windows.

793	## wording
794	alerts-08 | Alert text states the problem plainly and calmly, neither blaming the person nor playing down how serious it is.
795	alerts-09 | The alert title says what happened, where and why, specifically and briefly.
796	alerts-10 | An alert title is never a bare 'Error' or an error code.
797	alerts-11 | An alert title fits in at most two lines.
798	alerts-12 | A full-sentence alert title is sentence-case with a closing full stop; a fragment title is title-case with no closing punctuation.
799	alerts-13 | Add explanatory text under the alert title only when it tells the person something the title does not.
800	alerts-14 | Explanatory alert text is brief, in full sentences, sentence-case and punctuated.
801	alerts-15 | Alert text does not describe what each button does; the button titles carry that.
802	alerts-16 | When alert text must point to a button, it says 'choose' and names the button by its exact title, unquoted.
803	alerts-18 | Alert buttons are titled with one or two words naming their result, verbs tied to the alert text, e.g. 'Reply' or 'Ignore'.
804	alerts-19 | 'OK' is used only in alerts that just inform; 'Yes' and 'No' are never button titles.
805	alerts-20 | The button that abandons the alert's action is titled exactly 'Cancel'.
806	alerts-21 | Button titles are sentence-case and end without punctuation.
807	alerts-22 | In an alert that confirms an action, the default button names the action ('Erase', 'Delete', 'Convert') instead of 'OK'.
808	alerts-30 | A one-button alert whose button is the default titles it 'Done', not 'Cancel'.
809	boxes-03 | Title a box when the relation between its contents needs explaining; the title also tells screen-reader users what follows.
810	boxes-04 | Write box titles as short phrases in sentence case without ending punctuation, except a colon in a settings pane.
811	buttons-12 | Choose a text label over an icon whenever a couple of words explain the action better than a picture.
812	buttons-13 | Button text is a few words in title case, normally beginning with the verb for the action, e.g. 'Add to Cart'.
813	buttons-18 | A button whose action needs more input in another window, dialog or app ends its title with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Edit…'; one that acts immediately has none.
814	buttons-23*M | Do not put a caption beside view-attached add/remove buttons; their position next to the view explains them.
815	buttons-29*M | Do not caption the help button; the question mark is self-explanatory.
816	charting-data-08 | Add titles, subtitles, annotations or a one-line summary headline that state the chart's main takeaway.
817	charts-07 | Give every chart a title and labels that say what it shows and what it is for, so screen-reader users and everyone else know its purpose before exploring it.
818	charts-08 | State the chart's key takeaway in text next to it (a title or subtitle such as the expected rain in the next hour) so nobody has to read the marks to get it.
819	charts-26 | Describe data with actual numbers, not interpretive words like 'rapidly', 'gradually' or 'almost'.
820	charts-27 | Spell out dates and units in descriptions: 'June 6' rather than '6/6', '60 minutes' or '60 meters' rather than '60m'.
821	combo-boxes-03 | Write field labels in title case followed by a colon (e.g. 'Font Size:').
822	context-menus-06 | Name each submenu so its contents can be guessed before it opens.
823	context-menus-12 | Context menus normally have no title; add one only when it clarifies scope, e.g. stating how many selected items the command will affect.
824	design-principles-18 | Use exactly the words a concept or control label needs, and no more.
825	disclosure-controls-02 | A disclosure triangle has a label naming what it shows or hides, e.g. 'Advanced Options'.
826	dock-menus-01*M | Dock menu items have short labels and are grouped in a logical order, like any menu.
827	edit-menus-11 | Custom edit commands are labelled with a verb or short verb phrase.
828	entering-data-03 | Every field states what it wants, through a label such as 'Email' or an example prompt such as 'username@company.com'.
829	file-management-17 | The confirm button of an open dialog names the actual task when it differs from opening, e.g. 'Insert'.
830	file-management-19 | A new document is called 'Untitled' until the person names it.
831	icons-27*M | When a file type's extension is unfamiliar, label its document icon with a short descriptive word instead (e.g. 'scene' rather than 'scn').
832	inclusion-02 | Keep the text's tone clear, direct and respectful, avoiding an academic register that implies a required level of education.
833	inclusion-03 | Address the reader as 'you'; never call them 'the user' or 'the player' in visible text.
834	inclusion-04 | Use 'we' and 'our' only to mean the software or its maker, never to suggest a shared relationship with the reader.
835	inclusion-05 | Prefer plain words to jargon; where a technical term is unavoidable, define it first and make the definition easy to find.
836	inclusion-06 | Do not use idioms or slang in interface text (e.g. 'grandfathered in'); state the meaning plainly so it translates.
837	inclusion-07 | Leave jokes out of interface text unless there is a strong reason, as they translate badly and wear thin on repetition.
838	inclusion-10 | Write text without gendered pronouns where gender is irrelevant (e.g. 'Subscribers can post recipes' rather than 'his or her recipes').
839	inclusion-19 | Never use a disability as a metaphor for something bad, and include people with disabilities when showing people.
840	inclusion-20 | When writing about a person, lead with them and their goals before any disability, using the terms they use themselves.
841	keyboards-11*M | When a Mac shortcut is shown with several modifiers, they appear as Control, Option, Shift, Command in that sequence.
842	keyboards-12 | A shortcut on a shifted symbol is written with the symbol itself, e.g. Command-? and not Shift-Command-/.
843	lists-and-tables-04 | Keep row text short; for long items list only titles and show the full content in a detail view.
844	lists-and-tables-06 | Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no ending punctuation.
845	lists-and-tables-07 | A single-column list without a heading gets a label or header saying what it lists.
846	menus-01 | A menu item that performs an action is named with a short verb or verb phrase such as View, Close or Select.
847	menus-02 | Menu item wording follows the same voice and tone as the rest of the app's text.
848	menus-03 | Menu items are written in title case: every word capitalised except articles, coordinating conjunctions and short prepositions, with the last word always capitalised.
849	menus-04 | Menu item labels drop a, an and the, e.g. 'View Settings', not 'View the Settings'.
850	menus-07 | A menu item that opens a dialog or asks for more input before acting ends with the ellipsis character (…), e.g. 'Save As…'.
851	menus-22 | A state-switching label that could read as a status gets a verb, e.g. 'Turn HDR On' rather than 'HDR On'.
852	notifications-07 | Give a notification a brief, specific title (headline, event name, subject); when only a generic title such as 'New Document' is possible, omit it and let the app name show.
853	notifications-08 | Notification titles are in title case with no full stop at the end.
854	notifications-09 | Notification body text is short, written as complete sentences in sentence case with normal punctuation.
855	notifications-10 | Pass the full notification text and let the system shorten it; never cut it off or add an ellipsis yourself.
856	notifications-12 | Do not repeat the app's name or icon in a notification's text; the system already shows which app sent it.
857	notifications-16 | Each notification button label is a brief title-case phrase naming what happens, without the app name, short enough to survive translation without truncation.
858	offering-help-05 | Help copy uses the platform's interaction verbs: on the desktop, 'click' and 'choose', never 'tap'.
859	offering-help-11 | A tip is one or two sentences of direct, action-led text saying what the feature does and how to use it.
860	offering-help-12 | Tips never advertise or sell, and never cover a feature other than the one in front of the person.
861	offering-help-19 | A tooltip says what the control does, ideally starting with a verb, e.g. 'Restore default settings'.
862	offering-help-20 | A tooltip does not restate the control's visible name.
863	offering-help-21 | A tooltip stays within about 60 to 75 characters, allowing for growth in translation.
864	offering-help-22 | Tooltip text may be a fragment without articles to stay short.
865	offering-help-24 | Tooltips are written in sentence case.
866	offering-help-25 | Tooltips end without a full stop, even when they are whole sentences, unless the app's style says otherwise.
867	outline-views-03 | Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no punctuation, in particular no trailing colon.
868	panels-05 | Give each panel a title bar with a short noun or noun phrase in title case, e.g. 'Fonts', 'Inspector'.
869	panels-09 | Name menu commands for panels by the panel's title without the word 'panel', e.g. 'Show Fonts', 'Show Inspector'.
870	pop-up-buttons-04 | Label a pop-up button, or put a label before it, so its options can be guessed without opening it.
871	popovers-12 | Help text refers to the task or control ('Select the Show button'), never to 'the popover'.
872	progress-indicators-07 | A progress description says specifically what is happening, never vague words like 'Loading…' or 'Authenticating…'.
873	pull-down-buttons-07 | A pull-down menu has no title of its own unless the title adds information the button and items lack.
874	search-fields-01 | Give each search field placeholder text that says what it searches, e.g. 'Search messages'.
875	segmented-controls-08 | Segment labels are nouns or noun phrases in title case.
876	segmented-controls-09 | A segmented control with text labels needs no separate introductory label.
877	segmented-controls-11*M | Introduce an icon-labelled segmented control with text, or label each segment below it.
878	settings-14*M | Title the settings window with the current pane's name, or '<App name> Settings' when there is only one pane.
879	sidebars-08 | Title each sidebar group with a short descriptive label, dropping needless words.
880	sliders-07*M | Introduce a slider with a label in sentence case ending with a colon, e.g. 'Opacity:'.
881	sliders-09*M | Label the minimum and maximum ticks, and periodic ticks when the scale is non-linear, without labelling every tick.
882	tab-views-03 | Each tab is labelled with a noun or short noun phrase (occasionally a verb phrase) that predicts what its pane holds.
883	tab-views-04 | Tab labels are in title case.
884	the-menu-bar-07 | Name each top-level menu with a single word where possible so the bar stays compact and quick to scan.
885	the-menu-bar-08 | A top-level menu title of two or more words is written in title case.
886	the-menu-bar-10*M | The app name shown in the About item is at most 16 characters and carries no version number.
887	the-menu-bar-11*M | Hide App and Quit App use exactly the same short app name as the About item.
888	the-menu-bar-17 | The New command names the kind of thing it makes, e.g. 'New Event' or 'New Calendar', not just 'New'.
889	the-menu-bar-18 | A command that opens a chooser or asks for more input before acting ends its label with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Open…'.
890	the-menu-bar-33 | Undo and Redo labels name the action they reverse, e.g. 'Undo Typing' or 'Redo Paste and Match Style'.
891	the-menu-bar-34 | The command that removes a selection without touching the clipboard is called Delete, matching the Delete key, never Erase or Clear.
892	the-menu-bar-41 | A toggle item for a panel reads 'Show Toolbar' while the toolbar is hidden and 'Hide Toolbar' while it is shown.
893	toolbars-11 | A window's title names its content or area, not the application.
894	toolbars-12 | Keep a window or view title to a word or short phrase, under 15 characters, so controls keep their room.
895	windows-05 | Call every window a 'window' in visible text, never 'scene', 'pane' or another implementation term.
896	writing-01 | Settle on who the app speaks to and the vocabulary that suits them before writing its text.
897	writing-03 | Adjust tone to the situation: plain and direct for errors and payments, lighter for achievements.
898	writing-04 | Use easily understood words and cut every word that is not needed.
899	writing-05 | Write in simple language without jargon or gendered terms, with screen readers and translation in mind.
900	writing-08 | Label buttons and links with a plain verb (e.g. 'Send', not 'Let’s do it!').
901	writing-09 | Link text must name its destination (e.g. 'Learn more about UX writing'), never 'Click here'.
902	writing-11 | Fix one capitalisation style per element type (e.g. title case for all alert titles) and use it throughout.
903	writing-12 | In multi-step flows start with e.g. 'Get Started', advance with one consistent label ('Continue' or 'Next'), and end with 'Done'.
904	writing-13 | Drop 'my' and 'your' when context is clear ('Favorites', not 'Your Favorites'), and never mix perspectives.
905	writing-14 | Never use 'we' in interface text, especially in errors ('Unable to load content', not 'We’re having trouble…').
906	writing-15 | Name interactions by the device's input: 'click' with a pointer, 'tap' on touch.
907	writing-21 | Label each setting plainly and, if needed, add a line explaining what it does when on.

file.content:
path-controls-01 | Place a file-path bar inside the window's content area, never in the toolbar or status bar.
popovers-02 | Content needed only now and then goes in a popover rather than a permanent sidebar or panel.
popovers-03 | A popover points at the control that opened it and does not cover that control or content needed while using it.
popovers-10 | Size a popover to its contents and no larger.
printing-09*M | Hide rarely used print options behind a disclosure control labelled 'Advanced Options'.
right-to-left-01 | Text left-aligned in a left-to-right layout is right-aligned when the layout is mirrored.
right-to-left-02 | Text of three or more lines is aligned by its own script's direction, while one- and two-line text follows the interface direction.
right-to-left-03 | All items of a list share one alignment, following the interface direction even for items in another script.
right-to-left-05 | The digits of a single number, phone number or card number keep their order in right-to-left layouts.
right-to-left-06 | Scale numbers on mirrored sliders, progress bars and ratings, and ordered number sequences, run in reversed order, while each numeral's glyph stays unmirrored.
right-to-left-11 | Photos and illustrations are never mirrored for right-to-left; a direction-bound image gets a separate version instead.
right-to-left-12 | Images arranged in a meaningful order (by date, alphabet, rank) are laid out in reverse order in right-to-left layouts.
right-to-left-13 | Icons that depict text lines or reading direction are mirrored in right-to-left layouts.
right-to-left-16 | Icons that show something moving forward or backward are mirrored in right-to-left layouts so the motion keeps its meaning.
right-to-left-17 | Logos and universal marks such as the checkmark are never mirrored.
right-to-left-18 | Icons of real objects (clocks, right-handed tools) stay unmirrored unless they show a direction.
scroll-views-03 | When content continues past the view's edge, signal it, e.g. by letting a partly visible row or item show at the edge.
scroll-views-04 | Never nest a vertically scrolling region inside another vertical one (or horizontal in horizontal); crossing orientations is fine.
search-fields-04 | Rank results so the most relevant come first, and group them by category where that helps.
search-fields-17*M | A search that spans the window's content, especially in split views, sits at the trailing end of the toolbar.
search-fields-18*M | A search that filters the sidebar sits at the top of the sidebar.
search-fields-19*M | When search comes with rich suggestions and categories, give it its own sidebar entry leading to a search area.
search-fields-21*M | When the window narrows, keep the search field available next to the content it searches, e.g. above the list column.
searching-01 | When search matters, place the search field prominently, e.g. in the main toolbar.
searching-02 | Provide one clearly marked place that searches everything, adding local filters only for clearly separate sections.
segmented-controls-05 | Give all segments the same width.
settings-07 | Put options that affect only the current view (show/hide parts, sort order, filters) in that view, not in the settings window.
sidebars-02 | Let people choose which sidebar entries appear and in what order.
sidebars-06 | Show the sidebar by default.
sidebars-07 | Limit a sidebar to two levels; deeper data gets a split view with a content list between sidebar and detail.
sidebars-12*M | Collapse the sidebar automatically when the window gets narrow and bring it back when it widens.
sidebars-13*M | Do not put essential items at the bottom of a sidebar, where a moved window may hide them.
split-views-05*M | Give resizable panes minimum and maximum sizes so a divider can never be dragged until it effectively disappears.
split-views-06*M | Let users hide secondary panes to give the main editing area more room.
tab-views-08 | A tab view sits inside the window with a margin on every side rather than touching the window edges.
text-fields-05 | A field's width reflects how much text it expects, e.g. a postcode field is narrower than a street field.
text-fields-06 | Space several fields evenly so each label clearly belongs to its field.
text-fields-07 | Stack fields in a column and give related fields the same width.
toggles-09*M | Place switches, checkboxes and radio buttons in the window's content, never in a toolbar or status bar.
toggles-13*M | Show dependent settings as checkboxes aligned on their leading edge, with subordinate ones indented under the checkbox that governs them.
toggles-15*M | Introduce a group of checkboxes with a label describing the set when their relation isn't obvious, its baseline aligned with the first checkbox.
toggles-21*M | In a horizontal radio group, give every option the width of the longest label so spacing is even.
toolbars-01 | Keep the toolbar to a number of items each of which can be told apart and clicked easily.
toolbars-02 | Decide in advance which toolbar items move into the overflow menu, and in what order, as the window narrows.
toolbars-03 | The overflow menu appears only when items stop fitting, and at the default window width every item fits without it.
toolbars-09 | If the toolbar can be hidden for focus, hide it only in context and always provide a dependable way to bring it back.
toolbars-19 | A toolbar has at most one primary action and it sits at the trailing end.
toolbars-20 | The leading end holds Back and the sidebar toggle, then the title and an optional document menu (Duplicate, Rename, Move, Export); these items are not customisable.
toolbars-21 | The centre holds the common controls, which are the customisable ones and the first to collapse into the overflow menu when the window shrinks.
toolbars-22 | The trailing end holds items that must stay available (inspector toggles, search, the More menu, the primary action) and never overflows.
toolbars-23 | Group toolbar items into sections by what they do and how often they are used.
toolbars-24 | Navigation controls and critical actions such as Done, Close or Save each get their own clearly separated section of the toolbar.
toolbars-26 | Use no more than three groups of controls in a toolbar.
toolbars-27 | Put fixed space between a text-labelled toolbar button and its neighbours so adjacent labels or icons never read as one button.
typography-17 | Check every screen at the smallest and largest text or interface size and confirm the layout still fits and reads well.
typography-18 | Icons that carry information grow along with the text when the person picks a larger size.
typography-19 | At the largest text size a view should still show about as much useful text as at the largest standard size, wrapping rather than cutting it off.
typography-20 | Inside a scrolling area, text is cut short only when the full text can be opened elsewhere.
typography-21 | When large text crowds a row, move secondary items such as timestamps and icons below the text instead of beside it.
typography-22 | Multi-column text drops to fewer columns as the text size grows.
typography-23 | Primary elements stay at the top of a view whatever the text size, so their position never changes with scaling.
windows-10*M | Never place essential information or actions only in a window's bottom bar, since its bottom edge is often off screen.
windows-11*M | A bottom status bar holds only brief facts about the window's content or selection (e.g. item count, selected count, free space); more detail goes in an inspector.
writing-06 | Order each screen so the most important information comes first.
writing-07 | Split text covering several ideas across separate steps or screens with a planned flow.

## messages
accessibility-27 | Avoid views or messages that close themselves on a timer; let people dismiss them with an explicit action.
alerts-01 | Show a modal alert only when the person must know something or decide something now; every alert must carry essential content and useful actions.
alerts-02 | News that needs no decision goes in the relevant place in the window (a status indicator the person can open for detail), not in an alert.
alerts-03 | Deleting an item the person can undo, such as a file or a message, happens without a confirmation alert.
alerts-04 | A rare destructive action that cannot be undone asks for confirmation in an alert before it runs.
alerts-05 | No alert appears at launch; news for the person at start-up is placed where they can find it without being interrupted.
alerts-38 | Reserve the warning sign in an alert for cases that truly need extra attention, such as possible unexpected loss of data.
alerts-39 | An alert confirming an action whose whole purpose is to overwrite or remove data (Save over, Empty Trash) carries no warning sign.
design-principles-08 | State why each permission is requested and what data is collected and how it is used.
drag-and-drop-06 | When a drop can't be undone (e.g. into a write-only folder), ask for confirmation before completing it.
feedback-04 | Use alerts only for critical, preferably actionable information, not for routine or minor news.
feedback-05 | Warn before an action that will lose data irreversibly in a way people might not expect.
feedback-06 | Don't warn when losing the data is the obvious, intended result of the action, such as moving a file to the bin.
feedback-08 | When a command can't run, say so and explain why.
managing-notifications-01 | Give every notification an explicit urgency level (passive for browse-later, active as default, time-sensitive, critical), mapped to the platform's equivalent priority or urgency.
managing-notifications-04 | Never raise a notification's urgency above what its content deserves; low-priority news uses the default or passive level.
managing-notifications-05 | Use the high-urgency level only for events happening now or within about an hour.
managing-notifications-06 | Promotional or marketing content is never sent as a notification unless the user has explicitly opted in to it.
managing-notifications-07 | Marketing notifications always use a low urgency level and never break through do-not-disturb.
modality-07 | Closing a modal view by any means that would discard user content first explains this and offers a way to keep it, such as Save.
modality-10 | At most one alert is on screen at any moment.
multitasking-05 | Post a completion notification only for an important or time-sensitive task the user started and then left; routine background tasks finish silently.
notifications-01 | A desktop notification carries one useful piece of information that can be taken in at a glance.
notifications-02 | Post at most one notification per event; never repeat it because the user has not reacted.
notifications-03 | Notifications report something; they do not give the user instructions to carry out later in the app.
notifications-04 | Errors are reported in an alert dialog (or in the window), never through a desktop notification.
notifications-05 | While the app's window is frontmost, do not post a desktop notification; fold the news into the open view quietly, e.g. add the new item to the list or bump a count.
notifications-06 | Notification text contains no passwords, private message bodies, financial or health details, since bystanders may see it.
notifications-11 | Supply a short, non-revealing summary in sentence case (e.g. 'New comment', 'Reminder') for when the system hides notification content.
onboarding-12 | Access to private data is requested during onboarding with a reason only if the app cannot work without it; otherwise at the first use of the feature that needs it.
onboarding-13 | Requests for ratings or purchases wait until people have used the app for a while.
popovers-13 | Warnings are shown in an alert, never in a popover that can be missed or dismissed by accident.
progress-indicators-04 | When an operation stalls, the app says what went wrong and what the person can do, instead of leaving the indicator frozen.
progress-indicators-10 | Cancelling an operation that loses progress first asks for confirmation, with a choice to resume.
writing-16 | An empty view tells people what they can do next and offers a button or link to do it.
writing-17 | Do not put information people need later only in an empty-state message.
writing-18 | Show an error next to its cause, without blame, saying how to fix it (e.g. 'Choose a password with at least 8 characters').
writing-19 | Leave exclamations such as 'Oops' out of error messages.
writing-20 | Pick notification, alert or inline message by the urgency of the news and whether it needs action now.
writing-24 | Put field validation errors beside the field, phrased as how to do it right ('Use only letters for your name'), never a bare 'Invalid name'.

## other
charting-data-02 | Use a chart only when it makes a point about the data, and make clear what people can learn from it.
charting-data-07 | Look at the data at overall, subset and single-point levels to find totals, averages, useful subsets or notable values worth showing.
charts-01 | Pick the chart form from the question it answers: bars to compare categories, parts of a whole or per-period totals, lines for change and trend over time, points for relations between two properties and for spotting outliers.
charts-02 | Overlay a second mark kind when it helps, for example dots on a trend line so single readings stand out while the overall trend stays visible.
charts-03 | Give an axis fixed bounds when its minimum and maximum mean something for every possible value (a battery level runs 0-100%), and let the bounds follow the data when values vary widely so the marks fill the plot.
charts-04 | Start a bar chart's value axis at zero so bar heights compare honestly, but let charts whose interesting differences lie far from zero (such as heart rate) start nearer the data.
charts-05 | Label ticks with round, familiar steps such as 0, 5, 10 rather than offset steps like 1, 6, 11.
charts-12 | Interaction such as scrubbing to read a value may add detail, but the chart's essential information must be visible without any interaction.
color-10 | Check that a colour carrying meaning (e.g. red for danger) sends the intended message in each culture the app targets.
design-principles-01 | At each stage, check that every part of the design serves what the product is for.
design-principles-02 | Concentrate effort on the few features people use most and make those excellent.
design-principles-03 | Study existing solutions and design what sets the product apart instead of copying them.
design-principles-05 | Let people reach features freely without locking them into fixed flows or modes.
design-principles-09 | Collect only data the product needs and guard it against misuse.
design-principles-20 | Treat every element, including wording and sound, as a deliberate decision.
design-principles-21 | Prototype early, drop what fails, and test in real-world use for reliability and speed.
design-principles-23 | Decide the feeling the app should give and let it guide design choices.
design-principles-24 | Consider each interaction, down to button presses and error messages, as a chance to express the app's character.
design-principles-25 | Never let flourishes slow people down in their task.
design-principles-26 | Judge the experience as a whole: freedom to act, safety to explore, familiar metaphors, smooth changes of context.
drag-and-drop-08 | Offer dragged content in several formats from richest to plainest (native object, then vector, then lossless image, then lossy image) so the destination takes the best it accepts.
drag-and-drop-17 | On a drop, take the richest offered format the app understands (the native chart object rather than its picture).
drag-and-drop-18 | Take only the part of dropped content the destination needs, e.g. name and address from a contact dropped on a recipient field.
drag-and-drop-22 | Keep dropped text's formatting when the destination supports the same styles; otherwise give it the destination's style.
entering-data-02 | Never ask the user for data the app can read from settings or the system, with permission where needed.
icons-06 | Choose icons whose meaning reads across cultures and languages, with gender-neutral figures where people are shown.
icons-07 | Put letters in an icon only when they are the clearest way to show the idea (text formatting), localise those letters, and supply a mirrored version of icons that suggest lines of text for right-to-left languages.
inclusion-01 | Review the app for whether it welcomes everyone, not only for whether it avoids offensive content.
inclusion-11 | Let people choose the look of avatars or characters themselves instead of assigning a gender.
inclusion-12 | An icon or picture standing for an unspecified person must not show a gender.
inclusion-14 | Examples and pictures of people should vary in background, body, age and ability and avoid stereotyped roles.
inclusion-15 | Use everyday, broadly familiar settings and objects in examples rather than signs of affluence.
inclusion-16 | Do not build features or prompts around experiences not everyone shares (e.g. security questions about college or a first car); use universal ones.
inclusion-22 | Internationalise the app (text, dates, times, money in the user's language and region) before shipping translations.
inclusion-24 | Check per locale that colours carrying meaning say the same thing in each translation.
launching-03 | If the app has a splash screen, show it at the start of onboarding or right after launch completes, not as a delay before launch.
multitasking-01 | The app can be interrupted or put aside at any moment, so it keeps the user's work and position saved and restores them when the user returns.
multitasking-02 | Activities that need the user's attention or participation (a game, a timed exercise) pause when the user switches away and continue from the same point on return.
multitasking-03 | When other audio interrupts, pause the app's own primary audio (music, podcasts) until the user resumes it, and for short interruptions lower the volume or pause briefly and restore it afterwards.
multitasking-04 | A task the user started that needs no further input (download, export, processing) keeps running to completion when the window is minimised or loses focus.
onboarding-09 | The app ships enough content to be usable at first launch without waiting for downloads.
onboarding-10 | Licence texts and disclaimers are kept out of the first-run introduction, or if unavoidable placed so they do not interrupt it.
onboarding-11 | The app starts with sensible defaults, and optional setup is deferred so people can work right away.
printing-11*M | Remember changed print settings with the document, or at least until it is closed.
right-to-left-04 | Number-heavy apps decide per locale whether Western or Eastern Arabic numerals and which symbols to show; others use the platform's number formatting.
searching-05 | Think about who else can see the screen before showing past searches.
settings-01 | Choose defaults that suit most people so the app works well without any adjustment, detecting what can be detected (e.g. performance) instead of asking.
settings-02 | Offer as few settings as possible.
settings-04 | Don't ask in settings for anything the app can detect itself, such as whether the desktop is in dark mode.
text-fields-12 | Number formatting follows the person's locale, never a hard-coded separator or symbol.
the-menu-bar-23 | Save the user's work automatically at intervals so nothing depends on remembering to choose Save.
the-menu-bar-67*M | The menu bar extra appears only when the user has turned it on in settings (optionally offered during setup), never by the app's own decision.
the-menu-bar-68*M | Assume the menu bar extra may be hidden by the system or the user and never depend on it being visible or at a known position.

## pointer
accessibility-19 | Every action reachable by a gesture (swipe, pinch, trackpad gesture) must also be reachable by an on-screen control or command.
charts-13 | When individual marks are too small to hit, make the whole plot area the target and let people sweep across it to read values.
collections-03 | Every item in a collection must be easy to reach and select.
collections-05 | Beyond select, edit and scroll, add further item actions only when the app needs them.
designing-for-macos-04 | Support precise pointer selection and editing down to single pixels where the content calls for it.
drag-and-drop-01 | Support dragging and dropping content wherever people might try it, since they expect it to work everywhere.
drag-and-drop-02 | Everything people can do by drag and drop must also be possible through menu commands or other non-drag means (e.g. Copy, then Paste or Move To).
drag-and-drop-03 | Dropping within the same container moves; dropping into a different container or another app copies; deviate only toward whichever outcome is least likely to lose data.
drag-and-drop-04 | Let people select several items and drag them together as one group.
drag-and-drop-09 | Let buttons and segmented controls activate when people hold dragged content over them, so they can drop into the view the control opens.
drag-and-drop-16 | Auto-scroll a scrolling destination while content is dragged near its edge, and stop once the drag leaves the container.
drag-and-drop-25*M | Let people drag content out to the file manager, saved in a format the app can open again (an event as an .ics file, text as a clipping).
drag-and-drop-26*M | Allow dragging a selection out of an inactive window without bringing that window to the front.
drag-and-drop-27*M | Dragging an unselected item from an inactive window must leave that window's existing selection unchanged.
drag-and-drop-29*M | Change the pointer during a drag to show the outcome: copy, link, item will disappear, or not allowed.
drag-and-drop-30*M | Let one press-and-drag both select an item and start dragging it, without a pause in between.
edit-menus-02 | The edit (context) menu opens with the platform's usual gesture, a secondary click on the desktop, never a custom interaction.
entering-data-08 | Fields accept pasted and dropped data.
going-full-screen-09 | Hidden toolbars come back through a familiar action such as moving the pointer to the top edge of the screen.
lists-and-tables-12*M | Clicking a column heading sorts by that column, and clicking the heading of the sorted column reverses the order.
lists-and-tables-13*M | Table columns can be resized by the user to reveal clipped data.
outline-views-07 | Clicking a disclosure triangle expands or collapses that node only; modifier-clicking it (Option on a Mac) expands or collapses it with all descendants.
outline-views-10 | In an editable tree, a single click on a selected cell starts editing it while a double click opens the item (e.g. click a file name to rename, double-click to open).
pointing-devices-01 | A mouse or trackpad gesture such as swiping between pages must do the same thing in every view of the app that it does elsewhere on the system.
pointing-devices-02 | Never capture or reassign gestures the desktop keeps for itself (showing the Dock, Mission Control, switching desktops); the app leaves them to the system, which users may have remapped.
pointing-devices-04 | Controls that hide themselves (for example playback controls over full-screen video) reappear when the pointer moves over their area or over the content, and hide again once it leaves.
pointing-devices-05 | A modifier held during an interaction (e.g. the copy modifier while dragging) alters the outcome in exactly the same way whichever input device performs the drag.
pointing-devices-23 | Give clicks and gestures their standard meanings: primary click selects or activates, secondary click opens the context menu, wheel or two-finger scroll moves content in any direction, pinch or smart zoom changes zoom, a rotate gesture rotates content, and swiping navigates back and forward between pages.
pointing-devices-24*M | On a Mac, leave the system gestures (Mission Control, App Exposé, Notification Center, Launchpad, Show Desktop, switching full-screen spaces, lookup and force-click Quick Look, tap to click) to macOS and never bind app actions to them.
pointing-devices-25 | Set the pointer shape to the one that matches what will happen: arrow by default, I-beam over editable or selectable text, open hand over pannable content and closed hand while panning, crosshair for precise rectangle selection, pointing hand over links, directional resize arrows over resizable edges, and the not-allowed shape when a dragged item cannot be dropped there.
pointing-devices-26*M | On a Mac, a drag shows the copy pointer while Option is held, the alias/link pointer while Option-Command is held, the disappearing-item pointer when the drop will remove the item, and the context-menu pointer while Control is held over content that has one.
popovers-09 | With a popover open, one click on another popover-opening control both closes the first and opens the second.
scroll-views-08 | While a drag-selection extends past a view's edge, autoscroll in the pointer's direction.
split-views-02 | Let users move items between panes by drag and drop, e.g. a message onto a mailbox in the sidebar.
steppers-03*M | Shift-clicking a stepper changes the value by a larger step, such as ten times the normal increment.
text-fields-14 | Hovering a field whose text is cut off shows the full text in a tooltip.

## windows-and-dialogs
alerts-07 | An alert has a title, optional explanatory text and no more than three buttons.
alerts-17 | An alert holds a text field only when the person's input is needed to resolve it, such as a password.
alerts-23 | In a row of alert buttons the most likely choice sits at the trailing end; in a vertical stack it sits at the top.
alerts-24 | The default button is always the trailing button in a row, or the top one in a stack.
alerts-25 | Cancel sits at the leading end of a row of buttons, or at the bottom of a stack.
alerts-26 | Mark a button as destructive only when its destruction is not what the person asked for; the confirm button of a deliberately chosen action like Empty Trash stays unmarked.
alerts-27 | Every alert that offers a destructive action also has a Cancel button.
alerts-28 | Cancel is never the default button of an alert.
alerts-35 | An alert that can recur offers a 'do not show again' checkbox.
alerts-36 | An alert may carry an extra content area only when it needs to show information the text cannot.
buttons-15 | A button that deletes or discards data is never the default (Return) button, even when it is the expected choice.
design-principles-06 | Every guided flow offers a visible way to skip or leave it.
designing-for-macos-02 | Every main window can be resized, moved, hidden and shown, and supports full screen.
file-management-03 | A custom file browser may open on the most relevant folder but still lets people move anywhere in the file system.
file-management-15 | Opening and saving files uses the system's own file dialogs unless there is a strong reason for a custom one.
file-management-16 | A custom open view offers recently opened files, filtering by criteria and opening several files at once.
file-management-18 | Saving offers a view where the name, location and, when several are supported, the file format can be chosen.
file-management-20 | The save view starts in a sensible folder for the document rather than an arbitrary one.
file-management-21 | Options that matter when saving, such as including attachments, can be added to the save dialog itself.
file-management-23 | When autosave is off, closing a document, quitting, logging out or restarting with unsaved changes brings up a save prompt.
going-full-screen-01 | Offer full screen for windows where people view media, present, or do focused in-depth work.
going-full-screen-03 | The app never resizes its own window to fake or accompany full screen; the window size is the user's and the system's.
going-full-screen-04 | Everything needed to finish the task (e.g. playback controls) stays visible or one pointer move away in full screen.
going-full-screen-05*M | In full screen on a Mac, the Dock (and menu bar) can still be revealed in the usual way.
going-full-screen-06 | When the user leaves a full-screen experience, pause anything time-based (slideshow, game) and resume from that point on return.
going-full-screen-07 | Full screen ends only when the user asks; finishing a video or switching to another app does not leave it automatically.
going-full-screen-12*M | On a Mac, full screen uses the system's own mode (its own space, camera-housing area respected), not a hand-made borderless window.
going-full-screen-13 | Going full screen never changes the display's resolution or mode.
launching-04 | On restart, bring back windows with their size, position and state, and views at their last scroll position and location.
managing-notifications-08 | Ask for marketing-notification consent in a dialog or view that says what kind of messages will come and offers an equally clear yes and no.
managing-notifications-09 | The app's settings window lets the user change every notification choice they made, including marketing opt-in.
modality-01 | A modal view is used only when it helps people focus on or decide something about their content or device.
modality-02 | A modal task is short and simple enough that people do not lose track of what they left.
modality-03 | A modal task does not contain its own navigation hierarchy; if it needs subviews they form one linear path.
modality-04 | Inside a modal view no button may look like or be confused with the one that closes it.
modality-05 | Media viewing and multistep editing can take over the whole window to cut distraction.
modality-06 | Every modal view has an obvious way out; on the desktop that is a button within the dialog's own content area.
modality-08 | Every modal view carries a title naming its task, plus guiding text where useful.
modality-09 | A modal view is closed before another opens; modal views are not stacked, except that an alert may appear over one.
multitasking-09*M | On a Mac, media playing in one window keeps playing when the user activates or works in another window; losing focus is not a reason to pause.
panels-02 | Use a floating auxiliary window for controls or details that act on the current document or selection.
panels-03 | Show an inspector, whose contents follow the current selection, in a panel or split-view pane; show an Info window, whose contents stay fixed, as a regular window.
panels-06*M | Bring all of an app's open panels to the front when the app becomes active and hide them all when it becomes inactive.
panels-08*M | Give panels no active minimise button.
popovers-01 | A popover holds a few closely related settings or facts (e.g. an event's date, time and calendar), not a whole workflow.
popovers-04 | Add Cancel/Done to a popover only when it clarifies whether changes are kept; otherwise it closes on a click outside it.
popovers-05 | A single-choice popover closes when an item is picked; a popover allowing several choices stays open until dismissed or clicked outside.
popovers-06 | Clicking outside a nonmodal popover keeps what was entered; only an explicit Cancel button discards it.
popovers-07 | Only one popover is open at a time and none opens from inside another; opening a new one closes the current one first.
popovers-08 | Nothing appears on top of a popover except an alert.
popovers-15*M | Let users drag a popover off into a free-standing panel that stays open while they work elsewhere.
popovers-16*M | A popover dragged out into a panel keeps the same content and arrangement so the user stays oriented.
printing-04 | Offer page range, copies and two-sided printing through the system's print dialog, and only when the printer supports them.
printing-05*M | Add app-specific print options as an extra section in the print dialog, named after the app.
printing-06*M | Offer a Page Setup dialog for per-document paper size, orientation and scaling when the app has document-specific page settings.
printing-07*M | Don't duplicate options the system print dialog already has, such as orientation or reverse order.
searching-10 | Use the operating system's own open and save dialogs, which bring their own search.
settings-06 | Reserve the settings window for general options people rarely change, such as window configuration, key mappings or account options.
settings-12*M | Disable minimise and maximise on the settings window; it sizes itself to the current pane.
settings-13*M | Switch settings panes with a fixed, always-visible toolbar that marks the active pane.
settings-15*M | Reopen the settings window on the pane people last used.
sheets-01 | In a sheet, Cancel (or Close) dismisses without keeping changes and Done dismisses after completing the task or saving.
sheets-02 | A Back button in a multi-step sheet only returns to the previous step and never closes the sheet.
sheets-03 | Use a separate window or full screen rather than a sheet for long or complex tasks such as editing a document.
sheets-04 | Never stack sheets: close the current sheet before opening another, and reopen the first afterwards if needed.
sheets-05 | Supplementary tools the user needs while still working in the main window go in a non-modal panel, not a modal sheet.
sheets-06 | A sheet with Done always also has Cancel, or Back for a later step, so finishing is never the only way out.
sheets-07 | A sheet never shows Cancel, Done and Back at the same time.
sheets-13*M | Open each sheet at a size that fits its content without resizing, and allow resizing where users may want a larger view.
sheets-14*M | A sheet blocks only its parent window: the app's other windows stay usable and can be brought forward while it is open.
sheets-15*M | Tasks that repeat input and check results, such as find and replace, use a non-modal panel rather than a sheet.
the-menu-bar-21 | In a window with tabs, where Close becomes Close Tab, also offer Close Window to shut every tab at once.
the-menu-bar-24 | The first save of a never-saved document asks for its name and folder.
the-menu-bar-25 | When a document can be saved in several formats, the format is picked from a drop-down inside the save dialog rather than through separate commands.
the-menu-bar-30 | Printer choice, copy count and other per-print or global options are set in the Print dialog, not in Page Setup.
the-menu-bar-51*M | Zoom toggles between a content-fitted size and the user's size; it never enters or leaves full screen.
the-menu-bar-53*M | The list of open windows at the end of the Window menu is sorted alphabetically and omits panels and modal views.
toolbars-10 | Give every window a title that tells the user where they are and distinguishes it from other open windows of the same kind.
windows-01 | Every window's layout must keep working as the window is resized, so it can share the screen with other windows.
windows-02 | Open a separate window only where seeing two things at once helps (e.g. composing a message beside the inbox); otherwise stay in the current window.
windows-04 | Use the system's window frame and its close, minimise and zoom controls; do not draw imitation frames or title-bar buttons.

## wording
alerts-08 | Alert text states the problem plainly and calmly, neither blaming the person nor playing down how serious it is.
alerts-09 | The alert title says what happened, where and why, specifically and briefly.
alerts-10 | An alert title is never a bare 'Error' or an error code.
alerts-11 | An alert title fits in at most two lines.
alerts-12 | A full-sentence alert title is sentence-case with a closing full stop; a fragment title is title-case with no closing punctuation.
alerts-13 | Add explanatory text under the alert title only when it tells the person something the title does not.
alerts-14 | Explanatory alert text is brief, in full sentences, sentence-case and punctuated.
alerts-15 | Alert text does not describe what each button does; the button titles carry that.
alerts-16 | When alert text must point to a button, it says 'choose' and names the button by its exact title, unquoted.
alerts-18 | Alert buttons are titled with one or two words naming their result, verbs tied to the alert text, e.g. 'Reply' or 'Ignore'.
alerts-19 | 'OK' is used only in alerts that just inform; 'Yes' and 'No' are never button titles.
alerts-20 | The button that abandons the alert's action is titled exactly 'Cancel'.
alerts-21 | Button titles are sentence-case and end without punctuation.
alerts-22 | In an alert that confirms an action, the default button names the action ('Erase', 'Delete', 'Convert') instead of 'OK'.
alerts-30 | A one-button alert whose button is the default titles it 'Done', not 'Cancel'.
boxes-03 | Title a box when the relation between its contents needs explaining; the title also tells screen-reader users what follows.
boxes-04 | Write box titles as short phrases in sentence case without ending punctuation, except a colon in a settings pane.
buttons-12 | Choose a text label over an icon whenever a couple of words explain the action better than a picture.
buttons-13 | Button text is a few words in title case, normally beginning with the verb for the action, e.g. 'Add to Cart'.
buttons-18 | A button whose action needs more input in another window, dialog or app ends its title with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Edit…'; one that acts immediately has none.
buttons-23*M | Do not put a caption beside view-attached add/remove buttons; their position next to the view explains them.
buttons-29*M | Do not caption the help button; the question mark is self-explanatory.
charting-data-08 | Add titles, subtitles, annotations or a one-line summary headline that state the chart's main takeaway.
charts-07 | Give every chart a title and labels that say what it shows and what it is for, so screen-reader users and everyone else know its purpose before exploring it.
charts-08 | State the chart's key takeaway in text next to it (a title or subtitle such as the expected rain in the next hour) so nobody has to read the marks to get it.
charts-26 | Describe data with actual numbers, not interpretive words like 'rapidly', 'gradually' or 'almost'.
charts-27 | Spell out dates and units in descriptions: 'June 6' rather than '6/6', '60 minutes' or '60 meters' rather than '60m'.
combo-boxes-03 | Write field labels in title case followed by a colon (e.g. 'Font Size:').
context-menus-06 | Name each submenu so its contents can be guessed before it opens.
context-menus-12 | Context menus normally have no title; add one only when it clarifies scope, e.g. stating how many selected items the command will affect.
design-principles-18 | Use exactly the words a concept or control label needs, and no more.
disclosure-controls-02 | A disclosure triangle has a label naming what it shows or hides, e.g. 'Advanced Options'.
dock-menus-01*M | Dock menu items have short labels and are grouped in a logical order, like any menu.
edit-menus-11 | Custom edit commands are labelled with a verb or short verb phrase.
entering-data-03 | Every field states what it wants, through a label such as 'Email' or an example prompt such as 'username@company.com'.
file-management-17 | The confirm button of an open dialog names the actual task when it differs from opening, e.g. 'Insert'.
file-management-19 | A new document is called 'Untitled' until the person names it.
icons-27*M | When a file type's extension is unfamiliar, label its document icon with a short descriptive word instead (e.g. 'scene' rather than 'scn').
inclusion-02 | Keep the text's tone clear, direct and respectful, avoiding an academic register that implies a required level of education.
inclusion-03 | Address the reader as 'you'; never call them 'the user' or 'the player' in visible text.
inclusion-04 | Use 'we' and 'our' only to mean the software or its maker, never to suggest a shared relationship with the reader.
inclusion-05 | Prefer plain words to jargon; where a technical term is unavoidable, define it first and make the definition easy to find.
inclusion-06 | Do not use idioms or slang in interface text (e.g. 'grandfathered in'); state the meaning plainly so it translates.
inclusion-07 | Leave jokes out of interface text unless there is a strong reason, as they translate badly and wear thin on repetition.
inclusion-10 | Write text without gendered pronouns where gender is irrelevant (e.g. 'Subscribers can post recipes' rather than 'his or her recipes').
inclusion-19 | Never use a disability as a metaphor for something bad, and include people with disabilities when showing people.
inclusion-20 | When writing about a person, lead with them and their goals before any disability, using the terms they use themselves.
keyboards-11*M | When a Mac shortcut is shown with several modifiers, they appear as Control, Option, Shift, Command in that sequence.
keyboards-12 | A shortcut on a shifted symbol is written with the symbol itself, e.g. Command-? and not Shift-Command-/.
lists-and-tables-04 | Keep row text short; for long items list only titles and show the full content in a detail view.
lists-and-tables-06 | Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no ending punctuation.
lists-and-tables-07 | A single-column list without a heading gets a label or header saying what it lists.
menus-01 | A menu item that performs an action is named with a short verb or verb phrase such as View, Close or Select.
menus-02 | Menu item wording follows the same voice and tone as the rest of the app's text.
menus-03 | Menu items are written in title case: every word capitalised except articles, coordinating conjunctions and short prepositions, with the last word always capitalised.
menus-04 | Menu item labels drop a, an and the, e.g. 'View Settings', not 'View the Settings'.
menus-07 | A menu item that opens a dialog or asks for more input before acting ends with the ellipsis character (…), e.g. 'Save As…'.
menus-22 | A state-switching label that could read as a status gets a verb, e.g. 'Turn HDR On' rather than 'HDR On'.
notifications-07 | Give a notification a brief, specific title (headline, event name, subject); when only a generic title such as 'New Document' is possible, omit it and let the app name show.
notifications-08 | Notification titles are in title case with no full stop at the end.
notifications-09 | Notification body text is short, written as complete sentences in sentence case with normal punctuation.
notifications-10 | Pass the full notification text and let the system shorten it; never cut it off or add an ellipsis yourself.
notifications-12 | Do not repeat the app's name or icon in a notification's text; the system already shows which app sent it.
notifications-16 | Each notification button label is a brief title-case phrase naming what happens, without the app name, short enough to survive translation without truncation.
offering-help-05 | Help copy uses the platform's interaction verbs: on the desktop, 'click' and 'choose', never 'tap'.
offering-help-11 | A tip is one or two sentences of direct, action-led text saying what the feature does and how to use it.
offering-help-12 | Tips never advertise or sell, and never cover a feature other than the one in front of the person.
offering-help-19 | A tooltip says what the control does, ideally starting with a verb, e.g. 'Restore default settings'.
offering-help-20 | A tooltip does not restate the control's visible name.
offering-help-21 | A tooltip stays within about 60 to 75 characters, allowing for growth in translation.
offering-help-22 | Tooltip text may be a fragment without articles to stay short.
offering-help-24 | Tooltips are written in sentence case.
offering-help-25 | Tooltips end without a full stop, even when they are whole sentences, unless the app's style says otherwise.
outline-views-03 | Column headings are nouns or short noun phrases in title case with no punctuation, in particular no trailing colon.
panels-05 | Give each panel a title bar with a short noun or noun phrase in title case, e.g. 'Fonts', 'Inspector'.
panels-09 | Name menu commands for panels by the panel's title without the word 'panel', e.g. 'Show Fonts', 'Show Inspector'.
pop-up-buttons-04 | Label a pop-up button, or put a label before it, so its options can be guessed without opening it.
popovers-12 | Help text refers to the task or control ('Select the Show button'), never to 'the popover'.
progress-indicators-07 | A progress description says specifically what is happening, never vague words like 'Loading…' or 'Authenticating…'.
pull-down-buttons-07 | A pull-down menu has no title of its own unless the title adds information the button and items lack.
search-fields-01 | Give each search field placeholder text that says what it searches, e.g. 'Search messages'.
segmented-controls-08 | Segment labels are nouns or noun phrases in title case.
segmented-controls-09 | A segmented control with text labels needs no separate introductory label.
segmented-controls-11*M | Introduce an icon-labelled segmented control with text, or label each segment below it.
settings-14*M | Title the settings window with the current pane's name, or '<App name> Settings' when there is only one pane.
sidebars-08 | Title each sidebar group with a short descriptive label, dropping needless words.
sliders-07*M | Introduce a slider with a label in sentence case ending with a colon, e.g. 'Opacity:'.
sliders-09*M | Label the minimum and maximum ticks, and periodic ticks when the scale is non-linear, without labelling every tick.
tab-views-03 | Each tab is labelled with a noun or short noun phrase (occasionally a verb phrase) that predicts what its pane holds.
tab-views-04 | Tab labels are in title case.
the-menu-bar-07 | Name each top-level menu with a single word where possible so the bar stays compact and quick to scan.
the-menu-bar-08 | A top-level menu title of two or more words is written in title case.
the-menu-bar-10*M | The app name shown in the About item is at most 16 characters and carries no version number.
the-menu-bar-11*M | Hide App and Quit App use exactly the same short app name as the About item.
the-menu-bar-17 | The New command names the kind of thing it makes, e.g. 'New Event' or 'New Calendar', not just 'New'.
the-menu-bar-18 | A command that opens a chooser or asks for more input before acting ends its label with an ellipsis, e.g. 'Open…'.
the-menu-bar-33 | Undo and Redo labels name the action they reverse, e.g. 'Undo Typing' or 'Redo Paste and Match Style'.
the-menu-bar-34 | The command that removes a selection without touching the clipboard is called Delete, matching the Delete key, never Erase or Clear.
the-menu-bar-41 | A toggle item for a panel reads 'Show Toolbar' while the toolbar is hidden and 'Hide Toolbar' while it is shown.
toolbars-11 | A window's title names its content or area, not the application.
toolbars-12 | Keep a window or view title to a word or short phrase, under 15 characters, so controls keep their room.
windows-05 | Call every window a 'window' in visible text, never 'scene', 'pane' or another implementation term.
writing-01 | Settle on who the app speaks to and the vocabulary that suits them before writing its text.
writing-03 | Adjust tone to the situation: plain and direct for errors and payments, lighter for achievements.
writing-04 | Use easily understood words and cut every word that is not needed.
writing-05 | Write in simple language without jargon or gendered terms, with screen readers and translation in mind.
writing-08 | Label buttons and links with a plain verb (e.g. 'Send', not 'Let’s do it!').

# The merged rules. Each rule: id, title (the rule in plain words), example,
# win/mac forms (only where they differ), src (extracted ids without the
# "apple-" prefix), enf (where it will be enforced: list of (kind, text)),
# now (status, text). kinds: component, test-source, test-screen, test-app,
# review. status: enforces, partly, contradicts, none.

MS = "Not sourced yet: the Microsoft pages could not be fetched (README, Sources)."

RULES = []
def R(id, title, src, enf, now, ex=None, win=None, mac=None, plat=False):
    RULES.append(dict(id=id, title=title, src=src.split(), enf=enf, now=now, ex=ex, win=win, mac=mac, plat=plat))

C, TS, TSC, TA, RV = "component", "test-source", "test-screen", "test-app", "review"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- wording
R("WRD-1", "A button or menu item is a command: it starts with the verb that names what happens.",

   (RV, "The verb is the right one for the result.")],
  ("none", "No check on label wording (`uitest/uitest.go:180-212` checks only that a name exists). The library's own strings follow it (`table.go:595-605`)."),
  ex="\"The data is right\" → \"Mark Correct\"; \"Close the preview\" → \"Back\"")

  ex="\"Use the shipped default\" → \"Reset\"; \"Close the pane\" → \"Close\"")

  "offering-help-19 offering-help-20 offering-help-21 offering-help-22 offering-help-24 offering-help-25 offering-help-26 offering-help-18",
  [(TSC, "Fail a tooltip over 60 characters or ending in a full stop; fail a Button Explanation equal to the button's words."),

  "writing-09",
